title: How the eviction of an 87-year-old became Spain's 'last straw'
text:
It was an image of an 87-year-old woman on a stretcher, wheeled out by paramedics, that sparked a national movement.

She was not sick. Rather, evicted.

Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was stretchered out of her Madrid home. (Getty Images: Luciano Lima)

Maricarmen Abascal had lived in her Madrid apartment for more than 70 years.

She took over the lease her father signed in 1956, and enjoyed capped rent.

Then, in 2018, her apartment was bought by an investment firm.

The monthly rent soon soared from €500 ($811) to €1,650 ($2,678).

And Maricarmen, a pensioner with a disability whose monthly benefits total €1,350 ($2,192), was forced out in a court-ordered eviction.

A sign supporting the pensioner reads: "This system must burn. Maricarmen, you are not alone." (Reuters: Susana Vera)

For Spaniards, the eviction stirred up a deep-seated anger over a housing crisis that has only worsened in recent years.

Previously, protests included flotillas in the path of cruise ships and water pistol protests, as locals blamed tourism for housing unaffordability.

But it is Maricarmen's plight that could be the catalyst for real change to protect renters.

Fighting for a sanctuary

Days before her eviction, Maricarmen walked writer David Uclés through her Retiro home of more than seven decades.

She showed him the living room where she watched the coverage of former Spanish leader and dictator Francisco Franco's death in 1975.

She showed him the bedrooms where her mother and father drew their final breaths.

"I've always felt safe here," she told Uclés and Spanish newspaper El País.

" My home has been everything to me. I wouldn't exist without it. "

Maricarmen cries as she waits to see whether she will be evicted. (Getty Images: Fernando Sanchez/Europa Press)

The apartment in the upscale central Madrid suburb has been Maricarmen's sanctuary since she was 17.

But for the past eight years, it has also turned into a battleground in her David-and-Goliath fight.

After real estate investment company Urbagestión took over Maricarmen's lease in 2018, it first attempted to raise the rent to €2,650 ($4,313) — a 300 per cent increase.

That was later decreased to €1,650 ($2,678).

What followed was a drawn-out court feud over the new contract.

Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts. And with each appeal by Urbagestión, public attention on the case grew.

In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation.

Madrid City Council said later that Maricarmen had declined its offer of a place in an aged care home.

Then, in late September, the courts ruled in Urbagestión's favour.

Maricarmen would be evicted.

Maricarmen attending protests in May 2026, as interest in her case grows. (Reuters: Kacper Pempe)

A groundswell of protesters gathered at Maricarmen's address to protect the pensioner.

"Fight for your housing because we have the right to it," she told the crowd of hundreds on September 22.

The next morning, police officers beat down Maricarmen's door.

Reporters were cordoned off, and several demonstrators were dragged away.

Spanish riot police remove one of Maricarmen's supporters. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Maricarmen, 'the last straw'

Over the past decade, the average rental price per square metre in Spain has almost doubled, reaching €15.10 ($24.62) per square metre in August, according to real estate portal Idealista.

The Bank of Spain estimates that the country of about 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

Social housing in Spain makes up less than 2 per cent of the housing stock, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.

The European Union average is about 6–7 per cent.

Protesters did not back down as Maricarmen recovered in hospital.

Instead, they built a tent encampment in Puerta del Sol, one of Madrid's busiest landmarks.

"Maricarmen is one person, but there are many people in this situation," one protester said.

"We want the right to decent housing for all."

A 43-year-old teacher, Simón de la Riva, said: "Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now."

The encampment was led largely by Madrid's Tenant Union, with aims set out by spokesperson Valeria Racu.

Either the investment rental falls or the government falls: "Let it be very clear," she said.

The tents mirrored a similar 2011 protest in Puerta del Sol against austerity policies. (AP: Manu Fernandez)

Spain is expected to head to an election in less than 12 months.

Still facing heat over the Ceuta crisis, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has told the public he is working "against the clock" to bring new housing regulations into law.

The new decrees would be "for Maricarmen and for the millions of Spaniards who are suffering from the housing crisis".

"This is not a question of ideology; it is a question of humanity," Mr Sánchez said.

Maricarmen has become the symbol of Spain's housing crisis. (Getty Images: Fernando Sanchez/Europa Press)

Evictions ban and a rising movement

"We didn't think this was going to happen because situations like this happen all the time," Urbagestión co-owner Ricardo Alonso told conservative outlet Horizonte.

He said protesters had pursued and overwhelmed the company.

Eventually, Urbagestión relented.

After five days of protest and more than four hours of meetings, Urbagestión offered Maricarmen a new eight-year rental contract on September 28.

The contract came with a capped rent that would not exceed 30 per cent of her net income, similar to what she paid before the company took over in 2018.

A demonstrator burns a sign bearing images of the owners of Urbagestión. (Reuters: Alejandro Martinez Velez)

Mr Sánchez followed shortly after, with two new housing measures.

Among his promises were plans to stop "vulture funds" from buying in bulk then reselling properties at higher prices; an eviction ban on vulnerable tenants until 2030; and a new tax on seasonal rentals.

But Spain's Congress on Friday rejected those measures, heightening speculation that Mr Sánchez, who does not have a congressional majority, may call an early general election.

Demonstrators say they will continue protesting until housing measures are voted through. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Madrid's tent encampment shows no sign of packing up.

Elsewhere, more tent cities are popping up across Spain — in Barcelona, Seville and even the tourist mecca of Palma de Mallorca, in the Balearic Islands.

A tent at a Canary Islands protest bears a sign that reads: "Your Airbnb was my house." (Reuters: Borja Suarez)

In Madrid, the tenants' union said mass protests would go ahead on Saturday, local time, while crowds had already met outside Spain's assembly chanting "your profits, our misery", according to Reuters.

"There are years when nothing happens, and weeks when history is made. This could be one of them," the union said in a statement.

From her hospital bed, Maricarmen continued to champion those who had supported her.

"I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," she said.

It is a fight symbolic of the slogan some have used in the days since the pensioner's eviction.

A slogan that hints this fight is anything but over.

title: Concreter survives three deadly strokes, warns against ignoring symptoms
text:
When Dru Arnold was struck suddenly by slurred speech and a migraine, his first instinct was to try to sleep it off.

The 39-year-old concreter had no idea he was enduring a potentially deadly stroke.

And in the 24 hours it would take him to get to hospital, he suffered two more in quick succession.

After his wife called an ambulance, doctors found he had also been hit by a stroke two years earlier.

Seven months on since his February scare, he has mostly recovered, but his speech is still affected.

"There's a lot of people that have got it worse off than me," Mr Arnold said.

Dru Arnold says it has been an emotional journey for him and his wife Josie. (Supplied: Dru Arnold)

The fit and healthy Sunshine Coast man said he was unaware of the basic stroke symptoms until after his emergency.

"People that are just living their normal lives don't know much about strokes and about the symptoms and signs," he said.

One of his treating stroke nurses, Danika Lloyd, said Mr Arnold was "very lucky" considering how long it took him to seek medical attention.

"Being his age, most people probably don't think about that kind of stuff," she said.

Danika Lloyd says Mr Arnold was extremely lucky. (Supplied: Danika Lloyd)

Strokes do not discriminate

Queensland Health ranks strokes as one of the leading causes of death in Australians.

In 2024, strokes claimed 9,147 lives and, on average, affected someone every 11 minutes.

Sunshine Coast University Hospital (SCUH) stroke clinical nurse consultant Bailey McNamara said time was the most critical factor when it came to surviving a stroke.

The Sunshine Coast University Hospital stroke team, including Bailey McNamara, Jess Pyman and Robert Hopkinson, recently won an award. (Supplied: Queensland Health)

"We notice that a lot of people just sit on their symptoms at home," she said.

"By the time they get to hospital, sadly, they're out of that timeframe for us to be able to provide that hyper-acute therapy such as the clot-busting medication."

Mr Arnold was treated by the team at SCUH, which recently won an international award for how quickly it was able to treat the dangerous clots.

Lifestyle choices play a part

Ms McNamara said 80 per cent of strokes could be prevented.

She said it was important for people to eat well, exercise, monitor cholesterol and blood pressure, have regular GP check-ins and blood tests, and stay on top of any heart conditions or diabetes.

Binge drinking, smoking, vaping, and taking illicit drugs were among the major risk factors.

Stroke Foundation Australia's Kelvin Hill said strokes were increasing in people under 65.

Kelvin Hill says time can save lives when it comes to treating strokes. (Supplied: Stroke Foundation)

"Over the past 10 to 15 years, things like obesity and the rise in diabetes have also meant that for some people they're getting strokes earlier than what we've seen in the past," he said.

"We do need people to be more aware because every minute a stroke occurs, there are 1.9 million brain cells that die when they don't get the nutrients and oxygen in the blood supply."

Awareness could save lives

Mr Hill said people needed to be aware of the symptoms and act quickly.

"One in four people in their lifetime will be impacted," he said.

The symptoms of stroke include facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech, headaches, and brain fog.

The Sunshine Coast University Hospital recently won an award for its stroke treatment. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Mr Arnold said he wanted to help people understand what strokes looked like and how they should respond.

"It doesn't necessarily have to happen to you, but if you see the signs happening to someone else, you could save their life," Mr Arnold said.

"If we knew, I could have been better than I was, we could have got to the hospital a day earlier, and it might not have been so bad."

title: Inside the 'secret society' keeping the art of bellringing alive
text:
As dusk descends on Bathurst's Machattie Park in Central West New South Wales, bells can be heard tolling joyfully from the nearby All Saints Cathedral.

Inside the bell tower, six people rhythmically pull numbered ropes that have plush carpet grips.

These Bathurst bellringers are continuing a tradition that began in England in the 1600s.

"It's such a secret society, but such a lovely community," Bathurst ringing master Oriana Zanon said.

Loading...

The pinnacle of bellringing is a peal, a continuous ringing of the bells for hours.

It is both mentally and physically taxing, and many peal attempts fail.

"If you lose concentration for five seconds, then you've lost everything," Ms Zanon said.

Later this year, Ms Zanon will join ringers from central west NSW and Sydney to attempt a peal in the Bathurst church tower to honour 98-year-old Bathurst ringer Chris Bacon, reputed to be the world's oldest bellringer.

Bathurst's All Saints Cathedral opened in 2009 and features windows that showcase the ringing platform. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Hard to learn

The type of bellringing practised in Bathurst is known as "change ringing", which features brass bells attached to wooden wheels.

Music compositions known as "methods" resemble rows of code rather than music notes, and are written for six to 12 bell ringers.

Highly regimented and steeped in tradition, bellringing groups are known as "bands".

Players are assigned roles like ring masters, who run the band; steeple keepers, who maintain the bells; and tower captains, who guide and mentor their groups.

Taking up ringing in his 70s, Chris Bacon was drawn to the camaraderie between bellringers.

At 98 years old, Chris Bacon is the world's oldest bellringer. (ABC Central West: Murray McCloskey)

During the construction of the Bathurst belltower in 2009, experienced ringers from Sydney came out to the central west to train Mr Bacon and the band.

"They'd go back on Sunday night to pick up their normal jobs in Sydney," he said.

" I thought there can't be too many hobbies where people are prepared to do that for each other. "

Ms Zanon said to be still ringing at his age made Mr Bacon a "complete anomaly".

"It's really hard to learn. It can take 12 weeks to learn how to put two strokes together," she said.

"Normally, if you're 98 and ringing, you've been ringing since you were 12."

Oriana Zanon says it's important for bellringers to not lose concentration. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Training for a musical marathon

Just up the highway, the town of Orange is home to one of the world's most accomplished ringers.

Jim Woolford is the tower captain for the Orange Pealers and former master ringer at churches across the UK, and Sydney's St Mary's and St Andrew's cathedrals.

Having participated in thousands of peals for weddings, funerals or dignitaries, he fuels himself like a marathon runner, monitoring hydration and blood sugar levels.

"There is considerable mental and physical stamina required," Mr Woolford said

"At lower levels [of ringing] it is intense, people have to concentrate, but you reach a point where it is meditation.

"It is a delightful experience at a high level."

Orange local Jim Woolford is among the world's most experienced bellringers. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Mr Woolford trains other ringers in Orange using a TV screen in the belltower as a simulator.

"We have a practice on a Monday, another practice on a Tuesday and then we have one-on-one sessions using the simulator," he said.

"Because of all that, the standards are very high here."

Mr Woolford said he was focusing on preparing his younger ringers to teach the art themselves.

"There are lots of towers across the world where the bells are not rung anymore because there are no teachers, no people with the expertise," he said.

Secret handshake business

Some ringers are continuing personal traditions.

Bathurst steeple keeper Richard Hurford is a fourth-generation ringer, with his great-grandfather George Hurford the city's first.

"The only generation they didn't ring was my dad because of World War II," Mr Hurford said

Richard Hurford holds a picture of his great-grandfather, bellringer George Hurford. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

"My son has started ringing now. I feel part of a very ancient tradition."

Jim Woolford said the culture of bellringing was its defining feature.

"You have friends for life, wherever in the world they are," he said.

Ms Zanon said the craft remains a well-kept secret.

"You only know about bellringing if you're a bellringer," she said.

title: WA photos capture unseasonal rain and a hint of summer in September
text:
Western Australia's first month of spring was anything but straightforward.

The state experienced a mixed bag of weather, from unusually heavy rain inland to sudden bursts of summer-like heat.

Photos from our viewers from the month of September perfectly illustrate just how different WA's climate can be from one end of the state to the other.

Grey clouds and a rainbow over a field in the Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Karen Siegert)

The month began against the backdrop of a notably dry winter for a large part of the state.

The first major downpour didn't deliver the rain to Perth or the South West, but hundreds of kilometres inland.

A slow-moving trough drew tropical moisture into the Goldfields and the Interior, producing widespread cloud, rain and thunderstorms across the area.

It brought well above average rainfall for many locations that often only see about 5 to 15 millimetres of rain in September.

Yellow blooms in a field in Toodyay. (Supplied: Greg Brown)

Leonora picked up 59mm in the 24 hours to 9am on September 7, its wettest September day on record and nearly double its old record of 32.6mm from 1984.

The heavy rainfall led to flooded roads around Leonora and the closure of the Goldfields Highway and the Leonora-Laverton Road.

Despite the rainy conditions in the interior, it was drier at Perth's City Beach. (Supplied: Robert Rouse)

By the end of the month, the town had accumulated more than 136mm, a significant increase from its monthly average of just 9mms and smashing the station's old record of 83.3mm for the month back in 1904.

Temperatures soar

Mid-way through the month, there was a large temperature contrast across the country.

While south-eastern states shivered through below average temperatures, western parts of WA were sweating through more summer-like conditions as day-time temperatures soared up to 12 degrees Celsius more than usual.

A dog walks on a beach in Mandurah beneath glowering grey skies. (Supplied: Regine Andersen)

That heat was also thanks to that same trough system that had been driving storm activity through the interior.

A strong high pressure system to the south helped push the trough back towards the south-west coast, where it dragged warm air down from the north, which had observed 40C temperatures during the month.

The northerly winds saw temperatures soar across the southern half, with many locations challenging September records.

Beachgoers enjoy the sunshine at Cottesloe in Perth. (Supplied: Clive Addison)

Perth rapidly climbed to 30.3C on September 16, its first "30" of the season and its warmest day since April.

It saw residents flood to Perth's beaches for a chance to soak up the summer-like conditions.

Locals at South Perth foreshore, young and old, are enjoying the warmer weather. (Supplied: Greg Brown)

The heat didn't ease after sunset, with the temperature only dropping to 18.2C early the next morning, just shy of its warmest September minimum ever.

It wasn't just Perth that sweated through some warm nights

A pair of black swans, and cygnets, swim on the Swan River in Perth. (Supplied: Stuart Davis)

Nearly a dozen spots observed their hottest minimums for September, including Wongan Hills which only got down to 21C.

Murchison smashed its record from 1990 after dropping to a warm 19.8C and Cunderdin, Beverley and Badgingarra all broke their 15-year records.

Blue skies and warm daytime temperatures were seen in many parts of the state. (Supplied: Rod Lawson Kerr)

And the records kept tumbling during the day.

Katanning reached a toasty 31.8C on September 17, just tipping over its previous record from 2006.

Albany was one of the locations which experienced temperatures higher than usual. (Supplied: John Rich)

Rocky Gully South, North Walpole and Albany Airport also set new September records after reaching well above average temperatures for the month.

More unseasonal rain

The unusual rainfall events continued in the state's interior.

By late September, another moisture-rich system was generating heavy rain and thunderstorms across parts of the Goldfields, Interior and south-eastern parts.

Rawlinna Station, located between Kalgoorlie and Eucla, experienced late-September thunderstorms. (Supplied: Stu Parker)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder recorded about six times its average September rainfall, picking up just over 80mm.

The storm activity was another unseasonal event for a part of the state that is often dry during Spring.

Some viewers took to the road to experience the springtime conditions. (Supplied: Peter Randell)

That trough system was pushed back towards the south-west coast where it developed into a low pressure system, delivering rain across the weekend to central and southern parts of the state.

After a run of warm sunny days, Perth decided to foreshadow the gloomy ending of the AFL Grand Final by recording its coolest day of the month at a top of 17C.

A visitor enjoys the view from a platform at Bibra Lake. (Supplied: Gloria Daniels)

While the city missed out on much of the rainfall over the month, it received one final good dumping on the last day, pushing its total to just over 38mm, less than half its monthly average for September.

The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast an increased chance of unusually high rainfall across much of southern and central WA over October, which could make up for that lack of rain.

title: Graziers step in to fix damaged roads after incomes 'decimated'
text:
Samantha and Richard Maiden of Mt Gipps Station estimate they have lost more than a quarter of their annual business due to ongoing road closures.

The couple's sheep station, which also offers farm-stay accommodation in remote Far West New South Wales, has had about 25 millimetres of rain this year, closing its mainly dirt roads on and off for more than five months.

Sam Maiden is concerned about the safety of road users. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

While they waited for repair crews, Ms Maiden estimated they lost about $60,000 in revenue after having to cancel reservations with guests unable to get in on flooded roads.

"It's decimated the tourist business," the grazier said, whose station is located about 40 kilometres north of Broken Hill.

"We would be running at about 80 per cent down compared to this time last year."

Outback businesses blame app for customer downturn Inaccuracies with Live Traffic NSW are causing confusion and a loss of vital customers, businesses say.

Mr Maiden said the road is also heavily utilised by livestock trucks, which could easily tip over on the unstable road and prevent them from moving their sheep.

Getting graziers on board

Transport for New South Wales (TfNSW) has launched an initiative to hire graziers and station owners like the Maidens as contractors to help fix roads in the Far West using equipment they already may own.

Craig Matthews, director of regional road network maintenance for the west region, said the decision was due to three natural disasters in the area over the past six months.

Craig Matthews says the project aims to speed up road repairs in the Far West. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"The big challenge is we have 2,800km of unsealed road networks," he said.

"It's a very vast network of roads."

Mr Matthews said landholders wishing to become contractors would be paid hourly market rates through a tender process and would have to cover their own initial registration costs.

Red tape slowing repairs

However, graziers believe red tape is slowing road repairs because a trained spotter or safety supervisor must be present.

"We need to keep people safe, and we don't want people operating by themselves," Mr Mathews said.

Graziers say they have spent thousands of dollars for their own road-fixing machinery. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

However, Ms Maiden said it was "disrespectful" for TfNSW to think graziers did not already have the knowledge and safety requirements to work by themselves with their own workers.

Ms Maiden said the program was not fit for purpose as graziers did not want to take on "big contracts" and lengthy tender processes.

She suggested an "emergency response tender situation" where graziers who have the right equipment could be called upon to fix roads within 100km of them.

"We just want the road open. We don't want to make a billion dollars from it, [but] we need to be reimbursed for the costs and the time," she said.

Richard Maiden wants red tape to be cut to enable faster road repairs. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Mr Maiden said he would like to see the red tape cut, but graziers would likely resort to doing the work to fix roads by themselves, and another worker spotting, if the wait was months.

"I know they've got to have all the rules and regulations, but it gets to a point that [if] they make it that hard, nothing gets done."

title: Labor's working holiday visa policy risks regional seats, experts say
text:
After six months working as a chef in a Far North Queensland kitchen, Rocco Raseri should from today be eligible for his third year working holiday visa.

However, under the federal government's changes to the system, the number of spots up for grabs has gone from 31,000 last year, to now just over 5,000.

"With this uncertainty, probably I wouldn't even have done these six months of work," the 27-year-old Italian backpacker said.

"That is a lot [of time working] to not even get the opportunity to stay here."

Mr Raseri is one of thousands of casual seasonal workers who power Australia's winter holiday destination, and the country's third-largest foodbowl, in Far North Queensland.

He said if he had known his spot was not guaranteed, he would have made different choices, such as seeking sponsorship in a capital city.

"Probably just travelling in Australia to see as much as I can see, instead of staying six months in Cairns," he said.

"It's beautiful, but the goal was to get these days to apply for a visa."

Mr Raseri has finished his six months regional work to apply for his third-year visa. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Mr Raseri's change of heart is what businesses in backpacker-reliant regions fear most, and political analysts say it could cost Labor at the next federal election.

Vulnerable seats

Australian National University political marketing expert Andrew Hughes said working holiday visa changes put regional MPs in a tight spot.

Dr Hughes said the visa policy protected Labor's core city voters at the expense of backpacker-dependant regions nationwide.

Backpackers fill the jobs during peak seasons in Australia's third largest food bowl, Far North Queensland. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

The NTs Lingiari, Bullwinkel in WA, and several regional Tasmanian and New South Wales seats could now be in question, he said.

"It creates that wedge and that perception that the government has forgotten about the regions," he said.

However, Dr Hughes said Queensland votes were more vulnerable than any other state, particularly with "the rise of One Nation", and the far north's seat of Leichhardt would be ground zero.

Labor's Matt Smith won the long-held Coalition seat, spanning from Cairns to the Torres Strait, on a 9.5 per cent swing at last year's federal election.

It was one of seven new Labor seats delivered by Queensland, lifting its contribution from five to 12 of the state's 30 seats.

However, the LNP narrowly won the statewide vote by just over 1 per cent.

Political expert Andrew Hughes says Matt Smith is facing a huge challenge amid the new immigration changes. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Since then, One Nation has surged in popularity, polling 36 per cent in Queensland, ahead of Labor's 25 per cent, according to this week's Newspoll.

Dr Hughes said the visa policy was a "significant" challenge to Mr Smith's hold on the crucial Labor seat.

"It shows whether he's connected and listening to the needs of all his electorate or just those in certain areas which are more Labor friendly," he said.

" He's going to have to try and defend a policy which he knows probably in his electorate does not work. "

He said Labor would be keen to retain Leichhardt, which was a Coalition stronghold for decades under Warren Entsch who regularly crossed the parliamentary floor.

Focus on solutions

James Cook University political scientist Maxine Newlands agreed Queensland was "certainly unique" when it came to "bucking the trend" at federal level elections, making it worth major party focus.

However, she said regional MPs like Matt Smith did not need to publicly oppose the policy to bring confidence back to voters if alternatives were offered.

"It's got to be solution-led and it's got to be community solution led," she said.

Dr Maxine Newlands says Labor MPs will need to focus on solutions. (Supplied: Maxine Newlands)

She said Working Holiday Visa holders were the second-largest contributors to Australia's net overseas migration, placing them at the centre of the debate.

"The concern with this is obviously we're going to see a repetition of the shortage of workers that we saw during COVID," Dr Newlands said.

"[Leading up to the election] people are going to look and say to their local members, 'Have you done enough for us in the last three years?'"

Smith's plan

Earlier this week, Mr Smith told ABC Far North he was already having conversations with peak tourism and agriculture bodies in Cairns to come up with solutions.

"Then I can take that back to [Immigration Minister Tony Burke] and say 'Hey this is some of the stuff that's being thought of up here'," Mr Smith said.

Federal MP Matt Smith says he is already speaking with stakeholders for a way forward. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The current scheme, he said, was not attracting enough workers to regional Australia.

He said more than a third of an estimated 211,000 working holiday-makers were British, who no longer needed to complete regional work for extra visas.

"They're all hanging out in Bondi … they're not helping us out here, and that's where the pressure is being felt," he said.

" The important thing throughout this process is to make sure regions like ours continue to get the workforce they need. "

Mr Smith said increasing the Pacific Area Labor Mobility scheme was a viable option for the regions, but he would continue to work with stakeholders in the meantime.

Mr Smith says most backpackers are relaxing at Bondi Beach instead of working in the regions. (AAP: John Fotiadis )

"The last thing that any of us want to do is put the brakes on the tourism industry, particularly up here which has gone through so much over the last five or six years," he said.

Dr Hughes agreed the altruistic element of assisting Pacific nations tied into Labor's policy of assisting island nations like Tuvalu in the face of climate change and rising sea levels.

"Labor believes the working holiday changes takes some of the heat out of the migration debate, whereas I don't think it's achieved that outcome," he said.

title: How do I know my child is ready to leave the house on their own?
text:
By the time children are around 12 years old, many will begin to ask if they can go out to the local park, playground or shops to spend time with their friends without adult supervision.

This may happen more often during the school holiday period. They might say:

All of my friends are going. Can I hang out with them?

When a child first asks this question, it can be difficult for parents to judge whether their child is ready. Parents might want experts to give them a specific age recommendation, but children develop at their own pace and readiness varies.

This means there is no single right age when children are ready to spend time with friends, out of the house, unsupervised.

As the parent of three children, I've faced this situation myself.

So how do you know when it's okay to let your child go out on their own?

The importance of independence

Children need opportunities for independent activities to build wellbeing.

The freedom to go out with friends without adult supervision gives children the chance to explore, make choices and navigate unexpected challenges. It allows them to develop their autonomy, confidence and resilience.

What is FAFO parenting and does it work? Is FAFO the 1980s parenting style today's generation of kids need, rebellion against gentle child-rearing, or exhausted parents just throwing their hands in the air?

It can also help kids get more active. Adventurous outdoor activities with friends, such as bike riding, allow children to learn how to cope with potentially risky situations and uncertainty, which may reduce their chances of developing anxiety.

Research on children whose parents allowed them to travel and play in their neighbourhoods also found it may help them cultivate friendships and create a sense of community.

What are the main concerns?

While many parents and carers acknowledge the benefits of letting their child have more independence, they may still feel nervous about the potential risks that come with it.

A 2019 New Zealand survey asked more than 2,000 parents about their attitudes towards risky play and children being out on their own, and the barriers that prevented them from allowing their children to be more independent.

The two biggest concerns were road safety (increased risks of traffic accidents) and "stranger danger" (children potentially having encounters with harmful adults).

So, with these concerns in mind, what are some things you can do to see if your child is ready?

Have a conversation

If your child asks to be out alone, you might start by asking them:

What makes you feel ready to be out on your own?

Your child's answer may give you a clearer idea of whether they're ready or not.

I've stayed at home alone before. I'm responsible. I think you should trust me enough to be able to do this on my own.

Evaluate their readiness

There are a number of things to consider when deciding if your child is capable.

Loading...

First, is your child aware of their surroundings? Do they notice potential hazards? For instance, would they notice if a storm was approaching and they needed to seek shelter?

Second, does your child have good judgement? Would they think clearly if they were faced with an unexpected problem, such as getting a flat bike tyre?

Third, is your child reliable? Do they follow instructions? Can they be trusted to return home at an agreed-upon time?

Agree on some rules

If you think your child is ready, it's important to set ground rules for when they're out. This might include your child agreeing to stay within a particular area, being home by a certain time, and communicating if they are going to be late. You might also ask them to stay with their friends the entire time they're out.

Start closer to home

For many families, it helps to begin with an activity closer to home, such as walking to the park and back. As trust and confidence build for both of you, your child can then be allowed out longer and further away.

It's also good to have a plan with your child about what to do if something goes wrong, they want your help or they need to contact you.

While it can feel daunting initially, independent time with friends without parent supervision helps your child to grow, develop and thrive.

This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: Complaint over senior NT public servant who ran private NDIS provider
text:
A senior Northern Territory public servant responsible for child and family services in Central Australia spent nearly three years as the sole director of a private National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) provider in Alice Springs, and for 15 months also owned a 50 per cent stake in the business's parent company.

The Department of Children and Families plays a significant role in the NDIS system in the NT, with the most recent figures from 2024 showing more than 300 children in its care had active NDIS plans.

An ABC investigation has confirmed public servant Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families, and held shares in the business's parent company, Japhin The Teacher Pty Ltd, from December 2024 to February 2026.

Life Aspects is registered to provide a range of disability services, including assistance with independent living and support coordination, an area that involves arranging other providers for people with disability.

Kudzai Mutsunge was the sole director of Life Aspects for almost three years. (Supplied)

The ABC has seen no evidence that any child in the care of the department was a Life Aspects client.

The department has referred a complaint about a potential conflict of interest to an internal integrity process.

Ms Mutsunge wound up her directorship and shareholding in Life Aspects earlier this year, one week before an anonymous complaint was sent to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission in March.

A separate complaint went to the Department of Children and Families in August, from the Alice Springs-based Disability Advocacy Service (DAS).

On August 21, the department told the service it had referred the information "through the appropriate internal integrity processes" and was coordinating with the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) "where relevant". The outcome of that process, if any, is unknown.

In response to questions from the ABC, the department declined to say whether Ms Mutsunge had declared a potential conflict of interest or sought approval for outside work, saying it could not comment on individual employment or conduct matters.

Kudzai Mutsunge ran the NDIS business Life Aspects while holding senior roles in the Department of Children and Families. (ABC News: James Elton)

The ABC understands Ms Mutsunge quit the department on September 11.

Ms Mutsunge said she did not "endorse or agree to the allegations or characterisations" put to her by the ABC about whether her roles presented a potential conflict of interest, and said she could not respond to further questions within the timeframe provided.

Under the NT public service code of conduct, employees must declare any perceived, potential or actual conflicts of interest in writing to their chief executive.

The department's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot said it had "zero tolerance" for a failure to declare a conflict.

Ms Broadfoot said that where integrity matters involved the NDIS, the department would also coordinate with the Australian Federal Police when relevant.

The NDIA said it could not comment on ongoing investigations.

DAS chief executive Scott Richardson said government officials needed to be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts, to ensure they "don't have access to participant information that they could then benefit from, or family could benefit from".

DAS chief executive Scott Richardson says government officials should be held to a higher standard on potential NDIS conflicts. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In a meeting in March, Ms Mutsunge reportedly told DAS staff that she was "operationally removed" from placement decisions, and denied any role in referring children to NDIS providers.

Do you know more about this? If you know more about this story, please contact the reporter James Elton on elton.james@abc.net.au, or jameseltonabc@protonmail.com

Department toughens conflict of interest rules

As well as written declarations, the public service code of conduct in force since 2022 requires employees to get written approval from their chief executive before taking paid work outside the service.

The department went further and endorsed its own conflict of interest policy on May 29, 2025, while Ms Mutsunge was still sole director of Life Aspects.

The policy required staff to consider their own interests and those of their family, identify any conflicts and report them. It made clear conflicts were common and not necessarily a problem, so long as they were declared and managed.

The Department of Children and Families has recently changed its conflict of interest policy. (ABC News: Will Green)

Then on June 12, 2026, three months after Ms Mutsunge had offloaded Life Aspects, the department policy was updated.

The updated version created a tougher rule, which is being phased in, that all staff must complete an annual declaration covering any business or financial interests, including any jobs outside of the department, and submit paperwork saying "nil" if they have none.

The updated policy also includes extra measures for "higher risk" staff, specifically identifying staff who could influence referrals to NDIS providers.

Mr Richardson said it was a "real concern" that the policy was tightened soon after his organisation raised the case with the department, and questioned if the new policy was a "rushed reaction" while investigations were still underway.

Life Aspects provided services for NDIS clients. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Ms Mutsunge held senior roles in the department before she quit.

In June 2024, a document published by the NT government said she was Director of Remote Families for the Central Australia region.

By March this year, she was using an email signature that described her as Director, Youth and Family Support for the same region.

The NT's Public Guardian and Trustee, which acts for adults under guardianship orders, told the ABC two of the people it represents had been clients of Life Aspects in the past.

The restructure and the business with no identifiable owner

ASIC documents reveal that Life Aspects was restructured over four days in late February and early March this year.

They show Ms Mutsunge set up two new companies and then signed away her directorships on the day each was registered.

She also transferred her stake in the parent company back to Japhin Nyengera, the man who owned the other 50 per cent of its shares, and who recorded the same Alice Springs address as her in ASIC filings.

The Life Aspects companies then passed to Freejoy Murukayi, a New South Wales man whose LinkedIn profile describes him as an electrical technician working for mining giant BHP.

He now holds the sole share in Life Aspects Investments, which owns Life Aspects, but ASIC documents show his shareholding is "non-beneficial", meaning he holds the business for someone else.

ASIC filings previously listed the new parent company's registered address as occupied by "The Trustee" at the same address Ms Mutsunge had used for Life Aspects, but the beneficial owner can no longer be identified from public records.

In March, Life Aspects listed a new place of business at an address on Todd Street, in the centre of Alice Springs.

When the ABC attended in September, the premises carried signage for a different NDIS provider. A director of that company said they had never heard of Life Aspects.

Life Aspects and Mr Murukayi did not respond to questions.

Internet domain records show Ms Mutsunge remains the registrant and technical contact for the Life Aspects website, using a private, non-government email address, at the time of publication.

Life Aspects is still listed as an active provider.

'Did not think disclosure was required'

On March 12, two disability advocates from DAS held a meeting with Ms Mutsunge to discuss the matter.

In a complaint sent to the department in August, obtained by the ABC, they set out what they say she told them.

"Ms Mutsunge confirmed she has not lodged a formal conflict of interest declaration regarding her interest in Life Aspects through any Departmental system," DAS advocate Lachlan Imhof wrote.

This address in Todd Street in Alice Springs is the current registered place of business listed for Life Aspects Pty Ltd, although an unrelated company is presently operating there. (ABC News: Will Green)

"She stated that because she felt she 'did not do anything' with the business and did not believe she personally benefited, she did not think disclosure was required.

"She said a verbal disclosure was made at some point to a former supervisor who has since left the department, which cannot currently be verified."

According to Mr Imhof, Ms Mutsunge said her husband was "heavily involved" in the operation of the business and that it had been "sold via Facebook" in August last year.

But company records show Ms Mutsunge remained the sole director of Life Aspects until March 2026 and held her beneficial shares in the parent company until late February.

According to Mr Imhof, she told the advocates that selecting providers and signing agreements sat with case managers and foster parents, not with her.

NT Public Guardian and Trustee Beth Walker said her office had no capability to check whether the directors or owners of NDIS providers were employed by government agencies, and that privacy legislation prevented other departments from releasing that information.

The ABC is continuing to examine cases of Northern Territory public servants holding interests in NDIS providers.

title: Diseases of the past like measles and diphtheria are making a comeback
text:
Contracting a case of measles and enduring the fever, cough, sore eyes and characteristic red rash was a common part of growing up before vaccination was introduced.

The disease was so rampant in Australia that anyone born before the late 1960s is thought to be immune, as it's likely they've already had the disease as a child.

Since then, Australia has eliminated the highly-contagious virus through a vaccination campaign and has held the status of an endemic measles-free country for more than a decade.

Vaccination helped Australia eliminate measles — but there has been a recent outbreak in SA. (Centres for Disease Control)

A recent outbreak in South Australia spreading within a school community has sparked concern from health authorities, but it's not the only uncommon disease that has recently spiked in cases.

Australia is also experiencing the largest diphtheria outbreak since records began, with the cases predominantly among Indigenous people in outer regional and remote areas across four states and territories.

So what's happening and why?

Where are measles cases coming from?

The World Health Organisation declared Australia free of endemic measles in 2014, meaning there is no ongoing local transmission within the population, although cases can still be brought in from overseas.

After decades of effective vaccination, childhood diseases once considered to be things of the past are rebounding. (Reuters: Lucy Nicholson )

South Australia's latest outbreak was sparked by the return of a traveller who contracted the disease overseas and had since spread it to three other students and an adult in their 40s, who was hospitalised, within the Brighton Secondary School community.

Contract tracing is being undertaken after the adult spent more than 24 hours at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital's emergency department.

The outbreak takes SA's measles total so far this year to nine, the highest since 2016.

According to SA's Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier, it was a "disappointing" development but not altogether surprising given anti-vaccination misinformation.

Professor Nicola Spurrier says she has seen children die from vaccine preventable diseases during her time as a junior registrar. (ABC News; Che Chorley)

"I have seen our vaccination rates year on year since the [COVID-19] pandemic starting to drop … I see what information is being provided in other forms other than the science," Professor Spurrier told the ABC.

" In my past practice when I was a junior registrar, I'd see little ones die from these infectious diseases and it's always been so wonderful when we'd get new vaccines. "

Why is measles coming back?

Adelaide University professor and epidemiologist Adrian Esterman said measles vaccine access was also a contributing factor to the sliding rates.

"It's things like parents being very busy, trouble getting to see the GP, I think it's more things like that rather than people hesitating to get their children vaccinated," Professor Esterman said.

He said cases of measles have also been surging overseas.

"Canada has now lost its measles-free status, the UK has lost its measles-free status, the USA is almost certainly going to be losing it shortly," he said.

" I hope we don't lose ours, it's not likely at the moment, but it's something that we don't want to see. "

Epidemiologist Adrian Esterman says decades ago, the diseases were regarded as "absolute killers" in Australia. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Professor Esterman said measles, diphtheria and even whooping cough, which saw a national spike in cases in 2024, are all examples of childhood diseases which are making a comeback due to declining childhood vaccinations.

"All of these various childhood diseases, they used to be absolute killers 80-100 years ago," he said.

"Most families had large numbers of children because they knew so many would actually die during the first year."

What's happening with the diphtheria outbreak?

The latest surge of diphtheria infections — the largest outbreak in Australia since records began in 1991 — has now risen to more than 600 cases, 22 of which were in SA.

Vigilance urged as diphtheria cases pass 500 There have been more than 500 cases of diphtheria across Australia this year, as governments work to mitigate the largest outbreak since records began.

The highly contagious bacterial infection, which affect the nose, throat, airways or the skin, is treated with antibiotics and vaccination is considered the primary line of defence against the disease.

SA Health said cases have been plateauing in recent weeks as more than 4,500 vaccines have been delivered to communities in the far north and south-west.

"Up in the APY Lands where we've had the majority of the cases, there has been really high vaccinations so we're extremely pleased with the community's response," Professor Spurrier said.

title: Golf club spends $30k on water changes, only for policy to change
text:
A golf club in Launceston is calling for compensation from TasWater after spending an estimated $30,000 on water infrastructure works in response to billing changes, which were then essentially reversed.

Mowbray Golf Club saw its water bill double from $20,000 to about $40,000 due to a TasWater policy change to charge based on the size of a water pipe connection, rather than sewerage usage, from July 1.

The charge was based on the club's 100-millimetre connection, which it says it only uses in drought conditions and instead relies on its own storage for irrigation.

In response, the club decided to sever the 100mm connection and connect its clubhouse and other services to its 50mm connection at significant cost.

The club says it decided to sever its 100mm connection on the advice of TasWater. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

It increased fees for its members by 10 per cent to help pay for the works.

Club general manager Hayden Roberts said they chose to go ahead with the works after being told by TasWater that reducing connection size was the easiest method.

"I know we're not the only ones that have done such," he said.

On Friday, TasWater announced a change in response to concerns from businesses and sporting clubs.

It would take fixed sewerage charges from $20,000 to under $1,000 and charge 100mm connections as 20mm connections, with refunds offered for bills paid since July 1.

The change came too late for Mowbray Golf Club, however.

"Everyone's standing here going, why did we spend all this money?" Mr Roberts said.

"I think it's only reasonable at this point that TasWater remediates these situations, whether it be credit or an outright refund of works completed.

"We've actually lost an asset in the process of this removal of connection."

TasWater says changes had 'unintended consequences'

TasWater contacted the club in response to the policy change but had not made assurances regarding compensation.

Callan Paske from TasWater says the changes had unintended consequences. (ABC News)

TasWater general manager of customers and community Callan Paske said the water authority was aware of other clubs and businesses that had made changes to their connections based on TasWater advice.

"We're working with those impacted clubs to ensure that we can work through what the final solution is for them," he said.

" We understand the customer impact … we need to own that and learn from it. "

The change in sewerage charging followed an inquiry by the Tasmanian Economic Regulator, which required TasWater to move from an equivalent charging method to a fixed and variable method.

This is similar to methods used in other states.

Mr Paske said it had disproportionately impacted sporting clubs and businesses, which was addressed by the change announced on Friday.

"What this shows is that in any tariff reform there is nuance and we need to fix those outlier impacts that are in unintended consequences of major change," he said.

Water infrastructure challenges remain

TasWater again faces a challenge in how to fund upgrades to its aging infrastructure.

The changes have hit its bottom line by between $7 million and $14 million, according to Mr Paske.

"We've got aging infrastructure, failing pipes, we've got growth that we need to cater for, and we've got environmental impacts that we're having that are not what Tasmanians want to see," he said.

The change came following discussions between TasWater, the economic regulator, councils and the state government.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was a "significant and lasing outcome" for businesses and sporting clubs.

Shadow treasurer Dean Winter said the government had the power to veto TasWater's corporate plan, and questioned why this had not occurred following successive significant price increases.

title: One Nation makes election promise to revive Victoria's timber sector
text:
Two years after sawmills fell silent in Victoria's native forests, the logging industry could be revived if there is a change in government at the November election.

While the Coalition and One Nation have committed to restarting native forest logging, which was shut down by the Labor government in January 2024, it is unclear what it would take to get the industry back on its feet.

One Nation's Narracan candidate Ben Lucas said the policy supported country-of-origin labelling laws on timber and wood products, and a self-funding model in which harvest revenue supported forest improvement and fire prevention.

He said the party would consult industry leaders and audit the millions of dollars Labor spent on the logging industry transition fund before settling on a new approach.

"I don't know if you're picking up on a theme here with One Nation, but we don't need to overlord and control everything — the industry are the subject matter experts," he said.

He said the party would incentivise the use of Australian timber in construction through a "local wood first" policy in government procurement and would ensure timber was extracted using a selective harvesting model.

"You can't take away the forestry industry from a town like Noojee and replace the economy with a truffle festival once a year," Mr Lucas said.

Pauline Hanson with Ben Lucas during a visit to Gippsland in August. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

But when pressed for details, Mr Lucas would not clarify how much it could cost or what would be involved in reopening native forests to logging.

"This is a broad policy and it's very open-ended, but with clear guidelines on how we want to do it and why we want to do it," Mr Lucas said.

"We've got the words on paper and if we get in, we can have some influence on how that happens."

Coalition policy in the works

The Liberal-National Coalition is still working through the details of its policy, but Nationals leader Danny O'Brien previously vowed to restore native forest logging.

Nationals MP Melina Bath, whose portfolio includes timber, said the coalition was finalising its policy but also backed a return to logging.

"We will be announcing a suite of packages and policies in relation to this," Ms Bath said.

"They're still going through a parliamentary process and we make sure … that we've done our costings correctly."

Victoria's Regional Development Minister Michaela Settle said restarting native forestry under a Coalition or One Nation government would cost Victorians.

"One Nation needs to explain how the litigation, timber shortages and bushfire risks that forced the transition have suddenly vanished, because they haven't," Ms Settle said.

"Labor is backing forestry workers into new jobs, growing local plantation timber and keeping forestry skills and experience in our forests to reduce bushfire risk and support better forest management," she said.

According to a 2026 Victorian Auditor-General's report, the Victorian government's decision to shut down the industry affected 1,000 workers and 200 businesses.

It found the Victorian government spent $1.5 billion on transition arrangements and 87 per cent of workers had retired or found new jobs.

But it found many had moved into part-time, casual or contract roles and it was "not clear if workers' new jobs meet their needs or are sustainable".

Ms Bath said a revived industry would "look different to what the Labor government shut down in 2024" and would need to overcome challenges, such as rebuilding the workforce.

Orbost District Chamber of Commerce and Industry secretary Garry Squires said any move to revive the forestry sector would be well received in the regions.

Garry Squires says rural towns like Orbost would love to see a return of native forest logging. (ABC Gippsland: Natasha Schapova)

"The reality is you can't just start big harvesting operations right across Victoria in a hurry, but start off slowly with thinning operations," he said.

"We've got this great resource of eucalypt forests across Victoria.

" There's a big demand for domestic firewood, which is not being met at present because thinnings aren't happening. "

Plantation plan

Victoria has more than 380,000 hectares of plantation forest, totalling more than 20 per cent of Australia's plantations.

Victoria also produces about one-quarter of Australia's plantation-grown wood, at a gross value of about $550 million each year.

Victorian Forest Products Association chief executive Andrew White said the sector needed a commitment beyond the election to develop a long-term industry plan.

"Capital investment in manufacturing is not cheap. And in order for there to be a viable industry, whether it's soft wood or hardwood going forward, we need that long-term vision," he said.

Mr White said the sector faced challenges, including balancing demand for hardwood from forests and softwood from plantations, along with managing public forests to protect against bushfire.

"We have a very small amount of hardwood plantations in Victoria … there's an opportunity to continue to invest in those types of plantations over the longer term as well, while we still manage our public forests for forest health outcomes and fire management," Mr White said.

title: AFLW round eight: Giant slayers: Bombers win their first game of the season after stunning comeback

Essendon have dragged themselves off the bottom of the AFLW ladder with an inspiring comeback seven-point win over GWS Giants in Sydney on Saturday afternoon.

title: The Roosters lost the 2025 grand final without her. This time, Tarryn Aiken won’t let title slip
text:
Roosters halfback Tarryn Aiken returns to the NRLW grand final after missing the 2025 decider with an ACL injury.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tarryn Aiken doesn’t lose her cool often. So when she does, you listen. “If she’s spraying you, you know we’re all doing something wrong,” says teammate Olivia Kernick. There hasn’t been much wrong with the Roosters this season, which means Aiken’s sprays have been few and far between. But they’ve certainly been memorable. “It happened in the Raiders game,” Kernick begins. Not the Raiders game just gone, where the Roosters won 20-10 in last weekend’s preliminary final to progress to their third grand final in three years. Kernick is referring to the round-three clash the Roosters described as a “loss in our eyes”, even though they won, and have remained undefeated all season. Tarryn Aiken speaks at a grand final fan day on Friday. Getty Images “It was pretty funny,” concedes Kernick. “It was pretty early on. We don’t really hear from her, she’s very calm, cool and collected on field.”

Advertisement

It’s difficult to find fault with an unbeaten season, but if you want to nitpick then that’s the match to look at. The Roosters have trailed for a combined 70 minutes and two seconds all season, but nearly half of that was during the round-three match in Canberra. It prompted the Tricolours to wipe the whiteboard clean and start their season all over again. “I think we probably learnt a lot about ourselves in that game, and what works for us as a team,” Aiken says. “We had gone away and experimented with a few things before that game. But after that game, we went back to the drawing board and worked. Spoke about what strengths are good for our team and as individual players and went back to our strengths as a team.” And what are those strengths? “Can’t tell you that,” Aiken says with a smirk.

Advertisement

Ask others, however, and they’ll tell you the Roosters are strongest when Aiken is calling the shots. “She’s the best half in the game,” says captain Isabelle Kelly. “She gets a lot of recognition, but the way that she can read the game, attacking-wise, and create situations for the people outside of her, is really incredible.” Aiken was a notable absence in last year’s grand final, having suffered an ACL injury in the last round of the regular season which ruled her out of the finals. The Roosters lost the decider to Brisbane in the final five minutes of the match. Tarryn Aiken is assisted from the field after injuring her ACL in round 11 of the 2025 season. Getty Images Jocelyn Kelleher and Corban Baxter had been admirable when filling in at No.7. But Aiken had been the team’s X-factor, and her loss cost them dearly. “To lose your halfback two weeks out from a grand final, it’s obviously insanely hard considering we had her all year,” Kelleher says. “I was lucky enough to be trusted with that spot. However, we are a lot stronger when she’s back. She gets through holes that don’t even exist, and she’s a genius out on that field.”

Advertisement

That ability to step up when the game is on the line was on full display last weekend, when Aiken slipped through a crack in the Raiders defence to score the clinching try. Loading For Aiken, who had helped orchestrate the Broncos’ premierships in 2019 and 2020 and then for the Roosters in 2024, missing last year’s finals was the hardest moment of her career. “It was a tough week for me, personally, missing out on finals and the grand final,” says Aiken. “Career-wise, that was definitely the hardest part, missing the finals last year and then obviously the lengthy rehab.” She’s a nervous spectator, which made it difficult to sit on the sideline and watch, powerless, as the premiership slipped away. title: Five men interviewed for the Newcastle coaching job. This is why the Knights picked Holbrook
text:

SportNRLNRL 2026 Five men interviewed for the Newcastle coaching job. This is why the Knights picked Holbrook Christian Nicolussi October 3, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One thing stood out when the Knights interviewed Justin Holbrook: his vision for the club was clear. Holbrook knew exactly how he wanted the team to play, how they should look and, most importantly, how they should attack. Loading When Adam O’Brien parted ways with the Knights in August 2025, Newcastle compiled a strong list of candidates to interview. Blake Green and Brian McDermott were already at the club as part of O’Brien’s coaching staff, and mounted compelling cases. Both men put a strong emphasis on tidying up the defence and knew which kids were going to make the leap into grade football.

So did Dean Young, who was polished, well spoken and working as an assistant at St George Illawarra, well before he was catapulted into the main job at the Dragons. Young placed plenty of importance on making sure the club’s pathways were in place. Man of the people: Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook Getty Images Then there was Brad Arthur, who was coaching at Leeds in the Super League. He had already proven himself in the NRL by taking Parramatta to the grand final in 2022. His two boys, Matt and Jake, were no strangers to the club, and Arthur snr knew how to get the best out of Newcastle’s new 10-year, $13 million man, Dylan Brown, who made his NRL debut at the Eels under BA. Newcastle chief executive Peter Parr, director of football Chris James, chairman Geoff Coburn, board member Tony Price and club legend Michael Hagan, who was coach when the Knights won their last premiership in 2001, were all on the selection panel. They loved what Holbrook had to say; how he wanted to tap into the attacking talents of Kalyn Ponga, Bradman Best, Dom Young, Fletcher Sharpe, Fletcher Hunt, Sandon Smith and Brown, to name a few.

Advertisement

The 1997 and 2001 premiership teams were known for their gritty, blue-collar defence, but they also had plenty to offer in attack, via the likes of Andrew and Matthew Johns, Robbie O’Davis, Matt Gidley and Timana Tahu. Holbrook had also won a Super League grand final in 2019 at St Helens, a one-team town in the north of England, which was a good comparison to Newcastle. Justin Holbrook addresses the playing group after Sunday’s preliminary final win put them into their first grand final in 25 years. NRL Photos He was working as an assistant at the Roosters, Sunday’s rivals, who are known for chasing success every year, and demanding the best from the best. Holbrook’s thirst for knowledge and success also stretched to the international game, where he had spent time with Mal Meninga at the Kangaroos.

A constant theme this week is how approachable and relatable Holbrook is. The panel wanted their coach to be able to talk to everyone, from the cashed-up surfies living in Merewether to the no-nonsense miners of Cessnock. Holbrook was also determined to tap into the old boys’ network, and remind them all that what they had done for the club would never be forgotten. Danny Buderus was one of the first Holbrook went to. The new coach made it clear what he wanted from him as an assistant coach before the pre-season commenced. The tears flow for Kalyn Ponga and Dylan Lucas as they celebrate Newcastle’s unlikely preliminary final victory. title: Stephen King didn’t want another Carrie remake. This is what convinced him
text:
A new Carrie is upon us, but she’s not exactly what you’d expect.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first glance, Summer H. Howell and Stephen King’s Carrie White have nothing in common. One is a soft-spoken 22-year-old Canadian actor. The other is a traumatised telekinetic teen who destroys her hometown in a vengeful rage. Related Article ★★★★

Review This is the most brutal retelling of Carrie yet They do, however, share one key experience: they both spent their first prom covered in blood. Howell missed her high school dance – or “grad” as they call it in Canada – because she’d been working. Little did she know she’d stumble upon a second chance while filming the lead role in Carrie, Mike Flanagan’s TV adaptation of King’s seminal horror novel. “I had a wonderful prom,” Howell says with fond reminiscence and a hint of trauma. “It feels like one big fever dream ... I had about 11 days covered in blood, head to toe. I did a lot of relying on other people and sitting, trying not to mess up my continuity … It was really cool to get to experience it in a way.” Loading The “Black Prom” is one of the most famous sequences in horror history. It began, of course, with King’s 1974 debut novel, which introduced the image of Carrie doused in pigs’ blood following a cruel prank. It’s the pivotal moment in a story about an outcast teen who faces relentless bullying by schoolmates and a fanatically religious mother before unleashing her telekinetic powers in a fit of destruction.

Advertisement

Equal parts horrifying and tragic, the scene has been recreated many times including in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film with Sissy Spacek and the 2013 movie starring Chloë Grace Moretz and Julianne Moore. It’s even had several incarnations in a stage musical. Sissy Spacek during the iconic “Black Prom” scene in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Alamy Stock Photo Chloë Grace Moretz wreaks havoc in the 2013 film version of Carrie. In other words, the story has been told – exhaustively. So, when Amazon Prime Video pitched Flanagan the idea of adapting Carrie for the small screen, the showrunner’s first instinct was to turn it down. Not only was it not on his King adaptation wishlist, he also generally avoids remakes and sequels, opting instead for fresh source material like Gerald’s Game and The Haunting of Hill House. Stephen King was also sceptical. The horror legend believed there was no need for more Carrie. “He said, I think it’s been done’,” Flanagan recalls. “And I said ‘I think I agree’.” The filmmaker wouldn’t proceed without King’s stamp of approval. But an idea kept niggling at him. “Teenagers today deal with cruelty and anxiety to a degree [Stephen King] never could have contemplated 50 years ago.” Carrie showrunner Mike Flanagan “I couldn’t stop thinking about it,” Flanagan says. “It’s been half a century since Stephen King created that character and that story in that world, but so much of what he was talking about is more relevant today than it was when he wrote it.”

Advertisement

“Teenagers today deal with cruelty and anxiety to a degree Steve never could have contemplated 50 years ago – that I couldn’t contemplate when I was growing up. I never went to school afraid I could be killed there.” When Flanagan had his “Carrie moments”, he notes that they also remained largely private. His “most vulnerable, humiliating and defining moments” weren’t preserved digitally forever, in full view on the internet. Teenagers today can’t relate. So what would happen if Carrie were dropped in the age of TikTok and rampant school shootings? Related Article Streaming The most exciting book adaptations coming to TV this year Flanagan, who’s renowned for his emotional, character-driven horrors like The Fall of the House of Usher and Oculus, came up with what he calls the “anti-Carrie”. While De Palma’s lead character was traumatised from the moment the cameras started rolling, Flanagan’s is more of an “unspoiled heart”. “We created a character who came into the world with trust, eagerness and openness – with a fearlessness socially and a genuine belief in the goodness of the environment around her. She then reacts to the realities we’ve all normalised in society for teenagers,” he says. This, it turns out, was enough to convince Stephen King. But with that hurdle overcome, the next presented itself: finding the new Carrie White.

Advertisement

Flanagan, along with King as an executive producer, searched for someone who embodied an earnest curiosity without being naive, and a vulnerability paired with hidden strength. More than 1400 people auditioned for the role, making it the biggest casting effort of Flanagan’s career to date. Mike Flanagan had no idea how they were going to find his perfect Carrie White. Then Summer H. Howell appeared. Robert Falconer/Prime They searched tirelessly until, finally, Howell emerged. She had never read or seen previous versions of Carrie, which ironically worked in her favour. After sharing countless self-tapes, Howell was offered the role – on April Fools’ Day. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight “I was just like, ‘What’s happening? What a funny joke that would be’,” she says. “I always assume with big projects that you’re up against a lot of people. But I just put it out of mind and did my own thing.” Her reaction was a combination of shock, honour and a fair deal of intimidation. Carrie is legendary, after all. “But because I hadn’t been influenced by any other version of her, I found it to be really fun,” she says. “I just tried to have a good time with it and enjoy the ride.” Carrie isn’t the only character to undergo a refresh. Adopting more of a YA slant, the series offers a glimpse into the home-life of other key characters, including Carrie’s mother Margaret White, famously played by Piper Laurie in the 1976 film. Here, she’s played by Samantha Sloyan and is no longer a monster. Rather, she’s a product of her own abuse.

Advertisement

Summer H. Howell (left) and Samantha Sloyan (right) in the new Carrie series. Liane Hentscher/ Prime “Where Sam [Sloyan] takes it is so heartbreaking, so beautiful and so human,” Flanagan says. “The late season scenes between her and Summer are some of my favourite I’ve ever witnessed on a set of mine in my life. I’m very interested in the cyclical nature of abuse and trauma, and the self-sustaining nature of that.” Carrie’s main bully, Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton), is given similar treatment. She isn’t just a “mean girl monster”; she’s reacting to her own deep well of pain, largely caused by her parents’ divorce (her mother is played by Heather Graham) and money issues. This is the source of her poor choices, such as filming Carrie sobbing in the school showers after getting her first period. Instead of helping her, Hargensen chants “plug it up” and shares the footage on an anonymous account online, turning Carrie into the school’s laughingstock. “There really are no monsters in frame, at least not in the beginning,” Flanagan says. “And if we ever meet a monster, we get to see how they’re made.” Chris Hargensen, played by Alison Thornton (right) doesn’t simply play a “mean girl monster” in Mike Flanagan’s version of Carrie. Robert Falconer/Prime As horrific as scenes like this sound, it’s actually not that far off the experience of many contemporary US teens. Flanagan opened his writers’ room to actual high schoolers to hear their lived experience of bullying, gun violence and social media. Demonstrating the human side of horror is signature Flanagan. But it’s also something he picked up from King, who he describes as a “humanist and optimist”.

title: The common viral infections that are responsible for one in eight cancers
text:
in brief A new global analysis has revealed that 12 per cent of cancer is caused by pathogenic infection.

Just four viruses and one bacteria are responsible, opening new pathways for cancer prevention.

Roughly one in every eight cancer cases diagnosed worldwide is triggered by common viral and bacterial infections, rather than inherited genetics or lifestyle factors.

A major global analysis by the World Health Organization body, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, has found that an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 were directly caused by 12 carcinogenic pathogens.

While developing cancer is often viewed as unpredictable, the findings highlight the fact that millions of cases worldwide come from transmissible infections — which are largely preventable.

In an analysis for The Conversation, Dr John La Marca and Dr Sarah Diepstraten, senior research officers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, noted that the vast majority of these cancer diagnoses are driven by just a handful of pathogens.

"Four viruses and one bacteria were responsible for 12% of the world's cancer cases in 2024," they wrote.
