Kate Broun, deputy chair of Cancer Council’s Cancer Screening and Immunisation Committee, told SBS News that vaccinations and screenings can reduce the risk of cancers.

How does an infection cause cancer?

Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow out of control instead of dying, and is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimates that around 170,000 new cases of cancer are diagnosed each year in Australia. Roughly 40 per cent of the population will receive a cancer diagnosis by the age of 85.

The disease is caused when normal cell functions are disrupted, something that a virus or a bacterium can trigger.

Certain viruses, like human papillomavirus (HPV), insert their own genetic material directly into human DNA, hijacking cells and deactivating tumour-suppressing proteins. This allows the cells to divide uncontrollably.

"HPV can cause several cancers and other diseases in people of all genders," Broun said. "It is responsible for cases of cervical cancer, anal cancer, vaginal cancer, vulvar cancer, and penile cancer."

Other pathogens, like Helicobacter pylori in the stomach or hepatitis B and C in the liver, operate through persistent, chronic inflammation.

Decades of continuous tissue damage, cell death, and forced regeneration significantly increase the probability of copying errors, which eventually turn healthy cells malignant.

Others still, like HIV, weaken the immune system's natural surveillance mechanisms, which gives other, dormant viruses in the body the chance to activate and trigger tumours.

Which viruses cause cancer?

The report, published in Lancet Oncology, found that four primary pathogens were responsible for the vast majority of infection-driven cancers in 2024.

They were:

H. pylori: A common stomach bacterium responsible for 760,000 cases annually, mainly non-cardia gastric cancers.

HPV: Responsible for 750,000 cases, with cervical cancer making up 600,000 of those diagnoses.

Hepatitis B and C: Driven by chronic liver infections, these caused 360,000 and 160,000 cases of liver cancer, respectively.

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV): The virus responsible for glandular fever also drove 260,000 cases, with more research needed into its role in throat and stomach cancers, as well as various lymphomas.

Despite being the primary cause behind a substantial number of cancer cases, public awareness of the role pathogens play in the disease is limited.

La Marca and Diepstraten attribute this to the fact that many people carry these pathogens without knowing it.

"These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers," they wrote, noting that there is a long delay between infection and cancer onset, which blurs the link.

Preventing future cancer diagnoses

Despite the considerable global figures, researchers emphasise that infection-driven cancers represent the most preventable type on the planet.

Several successful public health interventions for many of these primary pathogens already exist.

HPV and hepatitis B immunisations offer anti-cancer protective properties, while hepatitis C antivirals and antibiotic treatment for H. pylori can eliminate chronic risks before issues develop.

"The HPV vaccine is safe and effective at protecting against HPV-related cancers and diseases," Broun said. "It is recommended and free for Australians aged 12 to 25 years of age."

"Even if you’re vaccinated against HPV, we encourage you to screen."

She added that people uncertain if they have been vaccinated against hepatitis B can speak with their GP about a blood test.

While there is no preventative vaccine against EBV, clinical trials are underway.

"Because these infections are largely preventable or treatable," La Marca and Diepstraten wrote, "scaling up global access to existing vaccines, screening, and antimicrobial therapies offers one of our most direct routes to cutting global cancer rates".

title: This animal escaped the zoo. Months later, she's still at large
text:
IN BRIEF Samba escaped with her sister Tango in March while being held in a temporary enclosure.

Zoo staff have been searching for the capybara for six months, responding to over 150 reported sightings.

Samba the capybara has been on the run for six months after escaping a temporary enclosure at Marwell Zoo in the UK.

Samba arrived at Marwell Zoo in Hampshire County on March 16 with her sister, Tango.

The pair were transferred from Jimmy's Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk.

Samba and Tango underwent "routine health checks" while their enclosure was being prepared, Marwell Zoo said in a statement.

The following day, while locked in a temporary holding area, the pair attempted a jailbreak.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Samba and Tango had other ideas ... and managed to escape from their new home," the zoo said.

Staff "quickly retrieved" Tango on zoo grounds. But nine-month-old Samba was "more adventurous" and has now been missing for six months.

The first sighting of Samba came a day after her escape in Owslebury, three kilometres from the zoo.

On 22 March, a dog walker spotted Samba lying in the sun on the banks of the River Itchen in the Colden Common area. Startled by the dog walker, Samba scurried down the banks and jumped into the river, making her escape by water.

She was spotted by the river the very next day.

Search efforts increased around the river, but the capybara's excellent camouflage secured her freedom.

Camera traps were placed in various locations where Samba had been spotted, including Twyford, North Twyford, Highbridge and Bambridge Gardens.

Rescue teams also conducted daily ground searches and thermal drone imaging searches — teams responded to 150 reported sightings.

Zoo insists new male not replacing Samba

On 7 July, Marwell Zoo introduced a new capybara.

Seven-year-old male Ripple was transferred from Blackpool Zoo and gradually introduced to the enclosure with Tango.

"His move is first and foremost about ensuring Tango's continued welfare by providing her with appropriate companionship," Marwell Zoo said.

The introduction of the new capybara raised concerns for Samba's future, but the zoo ensured she was not being replaced.

Ripple, a seven-year-old male capybara, has been introduced to Marwell Zoo as a companion animal for Tango, who was experiencing isolation stress. Source: Getty / Mark Metcalfe

"Welcoming Ripple does not mean we have stopped searching for her," they said.

"Our efforts to find Samba continue, and her welfare remains a priority for the team."

The last known sighting of Samba was on 11 August, near Bambridge Gardens.

Marwell Zoo said its team was "acting on a very promising lead" from photographic evidence of the now year-old capybara.

What are capybaras?

Native to South America, capybaras are the world's largest living rodent. They belong to the Caviidae family and are close relatives of the guinea pig and rock cavy.

They can live anywhere between four and eight years in the wild, and 12 in captivity.

Capybaras are semiaquatic herbivores, meaning they can live across savannas and dense forests and near and in freshwater.

They spend most of their time grazing or swimming and are highly social animals, preferring to live in large, close-knit groups of 10 to 40.

The average capybara weighs between 35 and 70 kilograms and stands about 60 centimetres tall.

Usually a slow and calm rodent, capybaras can have bursts of energy. They can reach speeds of 35km/hour when startled or threatened.

This speed helps them escape predators or, apparently, zookeepers eager to return them to captivity.

title: How daylight saving leaves one Australian border town operating on two different clocks

Border businesses near Tweed Heads and Coolangatta are preparing for booking mix-ups and confusion.

Same headache, new year.

In the wee hours of Sunday morning, daylight saving kicks in for the long Australian summer, when clocks skip forward by an hour from 2am to 3am.

But while the citizens of NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the ACT will enjoy an extra hour of sunshine after clocking off, Queensland remains the eastern seaboard outlier.

But for businesses in the NSW border town of Tweed Heads, as well as Coolangatta on the Queensland side, the issue is no joke.

Ellen Clark, a cosmetic nurse, recently opened a business in Tweed Heads and is bracing herself for late arrivals from her clientele, most of whom are in Queensland.

"It's going to be interesting trying to navigate that," she told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).

Previously, Ms Clark commuted to Brisbane for work from Tweed Heads, where her partner is based, but decided to set up shop locally after the birth of her first child.

"I used to have to stay on Queensland time while my partner would operate on NSW time," she said.

"It kind of came to my attention yesterday, and I was like, 'Oh my God, we're back here again'."

Sean McMillan is also new to Tweed Heads, having just set up a barber shop on Bay Street.

"All my systems go off bookings, so I'm trying to do some research, and I'm changing my hours a little bit to catch people on both sides of the border," he told the AAP.

"I'm sure there'll be people coming in an hour early or an hour late for bookings ... It's just one of those puzzles to work out."

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was not keen to buy into Tate's suggestion when asked about the issue by reporters in Mackay on Thursday.

"I've lived at both ends of the state, and I'm here for uniting Queensland, not dividing it," he said.

Queensland trialled daylight saving between 1989 and 1992 before being comprehensively rejected in a state referendum.

title: How one Australian state's corruption inquiry shook a major political party
text:
In brief NSW ICAC’s Operation Rosny examined alleged links between Liberal Party figures and developer Jean Nassif over donations and influence.

The high-profile inquiry exposed damaging allegations ahead of the state election and renewed scrutiny of party fundraising.

Phone calls packed with colourful language, meetings at Nobu, Fijian hideouts, all-day drinks at London pubs, promises of millions of dollars.

It was enough to fill out 38 sitting days as the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) sliced and diced a Liberal Party corruption scandal.

At the heart of the probe, the ICAC examined alleged collusion between fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and party powerbrokers including two brothers of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Jean-Claude Perrottet, Charles Perrottet and his wife Anita Perrottet endured days of grilling in the witness box.

In an inquiry dubbed Operation Rosny, the watchdog investigated alleged kickbacks involving Nassif and his company, Toplace, between 2020 and 2023.

Political donations from developers have been banned in NSW since 2009, yet the ICAC's widening net led to mentions of other powerful Liberals, including federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.

Former ICAC assistant commissioner and retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy rates Rosny one of the most impactful investigations in the body's almost 40-year history.

"You can already rank it as a very consequential inquiry," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.

"That is because it's taking quite a broad swipe into the machinations of party politics, the relationships between developers and politicians and where those intersections can go seriously wrong."

The inquiry began with a bang in July when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer launched her opening statement with the adage, "Money in politics, as in other spheres of life, has the potential to corrupt."

It ushered in weeks of forensic accounting and questions over embarrassing text exchanges about surveillance of mayors, sham contracts and fake arrangements spanning Beirut, London and Cessnock.

Twenty witnesses were called, including the bombastic Nassif, who dialled in virtually from his bedroom in Beirut, wrapping up on Tuesday.

Their memories — from a demure Jean-Claude Perrottet and emotional senior Liberal MP Damien Tudehope to brash lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood and a befuddled Anita Perrottet — were put to the test on the stand.

In their responses, revelations were unearthed, and admissions recorded that have damaged the Liberal Party as it heads to a state election in March.

"In terms of the Academy Awards, some would be given out for splendid attempts to shy away from the truth without very much success," Whealy says.

"Overall, the spectacle we saw was rather amusing, but then it wasn't amusing at all; it was really quite serious."

He says a number of witnesses have tarnished their reputations by not being open and honest with the commission.

Central to the probe was how the Reformers, a conservative Christian sub-faction within the Liberal Party, allegedly circumvented donation caps by setting up schemes to hide the money trail.

Taylor, who is not under investigation by the corruption watchdog, has denied making pledges to the ultra-conservative faction.

"I want to shake down Angus for 10K," the now sacked head of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, wrote in a message aired at the inquiry on Tuesday.

The opposition leader said "no payment was made" when questioned about a $15,000 "injection" and monthly $3000 donations to the Reformers.

Former NSW premier Nick Greiner doesn't want to wade into how Operation Rosny will affect the party whose federal executive he served until March this year.

But he credits the creation of ICAC in 1989, during his tenure as premier, as one of his most important contributions to keeping politics accountable.

"ICAC is now close to 40 years old, so in a broad sense it's been successful — and the fact that it's been copied everywhere is a fair indication of that," he says.

Its public airing of dirty laundry, which played a role in Greiner's own political demise, later brought down popular Liberal premier Gladys Berejiklian and Labor heavyweight Eddie Obeid.

Yet it has not been immune from criticism.

Greiner says the commission's sometimes spectacular binge-watching sessions were not all necessary.

"There's room for more common sense and discretion," he insists.

But he reserves sterner ire for how long it often takes the ICAC to establish a probe and make corruption findings, and then whether it recommends prosecutions.

The watchdog aims to have a report tabled in parliament within 180 days of receiving final submissions but in practice it takes much longer.

"Clearly the time frames are absolutely absurd," Greiner says.

"It cannot take years and years when you've got all the powers that ICAC has ... My general impression is it's way too slow."

Rosny was sparked when state Liberal MP Ray Williams used parliamentary privilege in 2022 to claim powerbrokers in his party were engaged in branch-stacking and improper local council dealings.

Whealy says the watchdog's invaluable oversight role should reassure the public that no matter how corrupt political parties might appear, there is always a comeuppance.

"There are some rotten apples around and (the ICAC) reinforces that notion but it doesn't destroy trust altogether in the political system," he says.

"It's a comfort to the community ... that there's a vigilant oversight body doing its job properly."

title: Rugby League's big weekend: The Koori Knockout, NRLW and NRL grand finals explained
text:
In brief The Koori Knockout, NRL and NRLW grand finals are all taking place this weekend.

Here's where to watch, when to watch and what to know.

Rugby league fans are in for a big weekend.

The NRL and NRLW grand finals, as well as the Koori Knockout, are on the agenda, as fans from across the country descend on NSW for the competitions.

The men's decider will see the Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights, while the women's match features the Sydney Roosters and the Brisbane Broncos.

In the Koori Knockout, which has already kicked off, 180 teams across men's, women's and juniors will compete.

Here's what to know ahead of the blockbuster weekend of league.

NRLW grand final

The women's decider will take place on Sunday 4 October at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

The NRLW officially started in 2018 and has since grown significantly from four teams to 12, featuring clubs across Australia and New Zealand.

The Roosters and Broncos are meeting at the grand final again after Brisbane defeated Sydney in last year's decider.

South Australia: 3.30pm

It will be shown exclusively on Channel 9 and its online platform 9Now.

NRL grand final

The men's match will follow the women's decider on Sunday evening at Stadium Australia.

The Knights will look to secure their first premiership in 25 years, while the Roosters are chasing victory after their back-to-back successes in 2018 and 2019.

NSW, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania: 7.30pm

Western Australia: 4.30pm

It will be shown exclusively on Channel 9 and its online platform 9Now. It will not be shown on platforms like Kayo or Fox Sports.

It seemed the match might go without pre-match entertainment after talks broke down with Australian artist Tones and I.

However, new NRL executive chairman Peter V'landys later teased a mystery 11-minute show.

"I've got to tell you it'll be the highest-rating 11 minutes you will ever see, because no one knows what it is, and we won't tell until the night," he told reporters earlier this week.

The event has also been recognised as a pathway for emerging Indigenous rugby league talent, with NRL stars including Latrell Mitchell, Cody Walker, Josh Addo-Carr, Jack Wighton and Greg Inglis among some of the big names who have taken to the field at the Knockout.

title: The age measure where Australian women outperform men three to one
text:
The Bureau of Statistics revealed this week that there were 188,421 registered deaths in Australia in 2025, which was 0.6 per cent higher than the previous year.

An ageing population contributed, with the median age of death for males at 79.7 years and 84.6 for females.

But what surprised me the most about the statistics is the extent to which females are outliving males, and in far greater numbers.

Among Australians who lived to 100 or older, women far outnumbered men: 2,392 women died last year, compared with 724 men.

That’s more than three women for every man.

So with an ageing population, it's no surprise to hear the corporate regulator ASIC say earlier this week that one of its key priorities this year is to deal with funeral insurance.

It says it continues to receive reports from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority and consumer groups about this type of insurance, especially where costs exceed benefits.

AI makes games more expensive

The Reserve Bank lifted interest rates this week to a 15-year high because it’s worried about rising inflation.

A key factor is how much businesses are passing on higher costs from the war in the Middle East to consumers.

In its official inflation report this week, the ABS said builders are passing on rising labour and material costs to customers via higher project home prices.

But it’s not the only industry passing on rising costs, and not all are related to the conflict.

The ABS also found games, toys and hobbies were 12.7 per cent more expensive in the year to August because price increases in computer chips are being passed on to consumers.

A global rush to invest in artificial intelligence is placing pressure on chip makers to keep up with demand.

So much so, MooMoo chief market strategist Tapas Strickland told me on the SBS On the Money Podcast that one US company was able to lift prices on chips that it rents out by about 20 per cent.

“What Nebius has been able to do, is put through price increases on four-year old Nvidia chips.”

Petrol stations look to electric

You know there’s a structural shift in the car market when traditional petrol companies move toward green energy.

This week Ampol has offered to pay $225 million to buy ultra-fast electric car charging firm Evie Networks.

The proposed merged group would become the largest public DC fast charging network by number of bays in Australia, with around 1,424 DC public charging spots, leapfrogging Tesla which has 1,230.

The deal, however, still needs ACCC approval.

The company says battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales have exceeded 20 per cent of new cars sold on average over the last five months, while public charging infrastructure has lagged BEV uptake.

This comes as the Electric Vehicle Council said a record 103,716 battery electric vehicles were sold in the first half of 2026, along with 54,241 plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.

It did however say EV transition for electric trucks and vans is happening at a crawl, with sales in that category representing less than 1 per cent of their respective markets.

title: 'People start to lose hope': Why more women are turning to elective egg freezing
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

At Jennifer Lynn Salcedo's 36th birthday party, she made an unexpected announcement — she was going to freeze her eggs.

"I didn't realise how empowering it was until I told people that I was doing it," Jennifer tells SBS News.

"I just never really spoke to anyone about actually doing it until I had my birthday ... and was like 'Hey, next week I'm starting this', and everyone just kept asking questions, everyone wanted to know, everyone was curious."

Salcedo says she had been considering egg freezing for around six years. Assisted reproductive technology (ART) involves retrieving and cryopreserving mature, unfertilised eggs — known as mature oocytes — for potential future use.

As women age and the number and quality of eggs naturally decline, freezing eggs can preserve the potential to use younger eggs later. But experts say it doesn't guarantee a future pregnancy or birth, and success depends on factors including the woman's age when the eggs are frozen and the number of eggs stored.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

For Salcedo, who says she has focused on her career in recent years and is currently single, egg freezing has provided an "insurance policy".

I've got a lot of friends that are having children, getting married and ... it's something that I've always wanted to do. It's just not been where my life has taken me.

For women considering egg freezing, the decision can involve balancing age-related fertility decline with the treatment's cost, physical demands and uncertain chances of ultimately using the frozen eggs — raising questions about how much reassurance the technology can realistically provide.

Why more women are considering fertility preservation

Australia's first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF) was born in 1980.

Today, ART is an established part of fertility care in Australia, with about one in 16 babies being born as a result of assisted reproductive technology, according to information published by the government-funded platform YourIVFSuccess.

Tamara Hunter is a Perth-based reproductive endocrinology and fertility specialist and believes more women are choosing to freeze their eggs for elective, or non-medical reasons.

She sees women like Salcedo daily and says she also turns away some young women.

"For whatever reason, they've asked their GP to perform a test of their ovarian reserve," Hunter tells SBS News.

"Then, they'll come in with that level, going 'I need to freeze my eggs'. [To] some of them, I'll say, 'Actually, you're 25, your egg count is within the normal range, there's no hurry. Why don't you come back and see me when you're 30?'"

But a woman's egg count is only part of the fertility picture. Ovarian reserve tests can indicate the number of eggs remaining, but they cannot measure egg quality or reliably predict a woman's chances of conceiving naturally.

A study led by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles, published last year, analysed elective egg-freezing rates in the United States between 2014 and 2021. It found the number of planned elective egg-freezing cycles increased from 4,153 in 2014 to 16,436 in 2021. Among women who froze their eggs between 2014 and 2016, 5.7 per cent returned to use them within the study's five-to-seven-year follow-up period.

But as elective egg freezing has become more common, researchers are still working to understand how frozen eggs perform over longer storage periods.

Hunter says it's unclear whether the amount of time an egg is frozen affects fertility.

We just don't have the large studies to be able to show that ... if you leave it [eggs] frozen for more than five years, it's going to be significantly degraded.

She says that's because data has historically drawn from the women who freeze their eggs for medical reasons, including women whose fertility was at risk from treatments such as chemotherapy, making it difficult to apply some of those findings directly to women who freeze their eggs electively.

Dr Tamara Hunter says it's unclear whether an egg's fertility is affected by how long it is frozen. Source: Getty / Science Photo Library

Modern egg-freezing techniques have also changed the evidence base. Vitrification — a rapid freezing technique — has improved the survival of eggs and embryos during freezing and thawing, although researchers say long-term outcome data for planned egg freezing are still developing.

But professor Georgina Chambers, director of the National Perinatal Epidemiology and Statistics Unit at the University of New South Wales, says modern freezing techniques have produced strong results for embryos.

"We get very good success rates from frozen embryos. How long can they be stored? We're not sure yet, but we know that with modern freezing techniques that are called vitrification ... the quality of those frozen embryos remains extremely high," she tells SBS News.

Chambers is also a lead author of a report which tracked ART treatment practices, pregnancy and birth outcomes across Australia and New Zealand.

The 2024 Australian and New Zealand Assisted Reproduction Database report recorded more than 113,000 IVF treatment cycles in 2024, resulting in more than 20,900 babies. It also found three in four IVF babies were born using frozen embryos, reflecting a clear shift towards frozen embryo transfers.

Chambers says freezing embryos can allow a woman's body to return to a natural cycle before the embryo is transferred, which can improve treatment outcomes.

"We allow the woman's body to return to a natural cycle, where her endometrium is ready to receive that embryo, and we get higher success rates from that process."

How much does egg freezing cost?

In Australia, elective egg freezing is usually self-funded, although costs vary between clinics and some medically indicated fertility-preservation treatment may attract Medicare rebates.

A single egg freezing cycle can cost several thousand dollars, with the total depending on what is included in the clinic's fee, as well as medication, anaesthetist, hospital and storage costs. YourIVFSuccess estimates elective egg freezing typically costs between $8,000 and $12,000 per cycle upfront, with additional annual storage fees.

The cost of using the eggs later is separate. The eggs must be thawed and fertilised to create embryos that are transferred to the uterus, creating further treatment and out-of-pocket expenses.

Jennifer Lynn Salcedo says she also experienced a hormone "crash" after the egg retrieval due to a temporary increase in her estrogen levels. Credit: Jennifer Lynn Salcedo

In September, Salcedo underwent her second egg freezing cycle via a private fertility specialist. Working in the banking sector, she was entitled to five days of family planning leave but admits the process was physically and emotionally taxing.

In my first cycle, I was just hungry, constantly hungry. I gained 7kg in that time from start to extraction, and I was like, 'Oh my god, my body's completely changed'.

Egg freezing requires women to administer daily hormone injections for about two weeks to stimulate the ovaries. The eggs are then collected during a procedure performed under sedation or anaesthesia.

"I was pretty much so bloated that I looked like I was six months pregnant," Salcedo says.

The 'egg count' test

Luke Grzeskowiak is a practitioner fellow at Flinders University's College of Medicine and Public Health and recently published a study analysing almost 1.4 million health records for Australian women.

The study found that anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) tests in Australian general practice increased more than 13-fold between 2011 and 2021. Women aged 30 to 34 recorded the sharpest increase, with testing rates rising almost 20-fold.

AMH is often marketed as a fertility test or "egg count" because it provides an indication of ovarian reserve — the number of eggs remaining in the ovaries.

"AMH testing can tell you about the quantity of eggs remaining, and the largest predictor of that is really just age-related. So, as we get older, there's a natural decline in egg count," Grzeskowiak tells SBS News.

The issue is it can't tell you anything about the quality, and it's really the quality that is the most important predictor of a potential good pregnancy outcome.

Grzeskowiak believes that rise in testing can be attributed in part to increased consumer marketing and ads about AMH.

"There's some interesting research that's published that's evaluated what's marketed around these tests, and what they find is a high level of misinformation around what AMH tests can and can't tell you and their usefulness or potential lack thereof," he says.

He acknowledges AMH testing can have a clinical role, including for people undergoing ART or cancer treatment and can also form part of the assessment of conditions such as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome — a hormonal condition that can affect the ovaries and reproductive health.

What happens to frozen eggs that aren't used?

As a clinician, Hunter says the rise in elective egg freezing also poses complex ethical questions around the storage and disposal of unused eggs.

We've got this unique irony where we're growing these banks of eggs, and at some point, there won't be enough room.

"So, we've got this opportunity then to talk to young women about, 'Well, you're not going to use them, would you consider donating them?'" she says.

"In that space, there are a lot of ethical and societal challenges: how do we compensate women who've frozen their eggs and paid storage every year for 10 years?"

Unlike IVF treatment for infertility, Medicare does not subsidise elective egg freezing for non-medical reasons. Source: AP / Thanassis Stavrakis

The rules governing how long eggs, sperm (also called gametes) and embryos can be stored vary between Australian states and territories.

Some jurisdictions regulate storage and removal, including for donated gametes or embryos and in circumstances where a donor dies. Other jurisdictions, including the Northern Territory, do not have specific ART legislation.

"In Western Australia you can store them for 10 years and then beyond that we have to ask, 'Do you want to dispose of them ... do you want to donate them?'" Hunter says.

We're not having those discussions with young women who are egg freezing, and that's a problem.

In June last year, health ministers called for a rapid review into ART regulation and accreditation following concerns about "safety, oversight and transparency" in the sector. The review followed two high-profile cases in which embryos were mistakenly transferred.

In September 2025, the review released 10 recommended areas for reform, including changes to how ART services are accredited and regulated.

The Department of Health says the new national standards aim to better align with state-based legislation and regulation, including requirements for the storage and disposal of reproductive material.

A transition to the new scheme is expected by December 2028, with the current regulatory framework to remain in place until then.

In a statement to SBS News, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) said it provides "ethical guidance for the use of ART in clinical practice and research" through its guidelines, which also set "out the ethical responsibilities of IVF clinics regarding stored gametes and embryos".

However, the NHMRC said the regulation of ART clinical practice is a matter for state and territory governments.

Meanwhile, for women like Salcedo, egg freezing continues to provide a sense of long-term security.

"I think when I get to 40, I'll probably decide if I want to choose to be a single mum and do that, but I'm leaving that decision until later.

"I think a lot of people start to lose hope, especially if you start to get closer to 40, but there are ways to achieve that."

title: New student visa crackdown comes with extra cost for course-switchers
text:
In Brief Students switching education providers will have to pay a new visa fee, expected to cost about half the original visa fee.

Student visa application fees have also risen from $1,600 to $2,000.

New rules for international students are in force, aimed at stopping so-called 'visa-hopping' by limiting course changes and curtailing how family members can join them in Australia.

Students wanting to change education providers will need to apply for a new visa, starting next year, which will cost over $2,000.

Labor's plan to bring net overseas migration down to a budget target of 225,000 by 2028 will be partly fulfilled by closing onshore pathways from temporary visas to student visas, Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill told a migration conference on Friday.

"People will no longer be able to apply for a student visa while in Australia from working holidaymaker visas, training visas, temporary employer visas and so on," he said.

The plan includes banning student and graduate visa holders from bringing their families unless they are on government scholarships, PhD students or from Pacific and ASEAN countries. The new family rules mean that dependants can only be added after their visa is granted.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Families already in Australia will be grandfathered as an exception as the government is not in the business of breaking up families already here," Hill said.

From July next year, students switching education providers will need to apply for a new visa, expected to cost about half the original visa fee, estimated at around $2,500.

The new visa will retain the original end date and can only be issued if students move into equivalent or higher qualifications.

International students who swap courses will have to complete 12 months instead of the current six while the new visa regime is set up.

"Australia welcomes genuine students seeking a premium Australian education but the government will not back down from seeking to manage the size and the shape of the onshore student market," Hill said.

Student visa rejections hit record levels in August at 35 per cent, up 12 per cent on the same month last year.

Students can extend their visa to complete a course if they fall sick, fail a subject or their course provider goes out of business.

After completing a course, they can apply for a new student visa, but it must be ranked higher in the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF). Moving from higher education to higher VET courses will not be allowed.

Independent MP Allegra Spender told SBS News that temporary visa holders have grown from 1.8 million to 2.8 million in a decade, which is supported by Department of Home Affairs figures.

"That's not sustainable, economically or socially," Spender said.

"International students bring enormous value. But in some universities their growth has coincided with a declining student experience.

"The government must get the settings right, and universities must build a shared campus life, so it's a genuine exchange. Limits to family visas for international students and restrictions on visa hopping are sensible. The question is why these settings are new," she said.

"Every migration choice is a trade-off, and Australians deserve a say in making them. The crossbench will take those trade-offs directly to our communities ... I suspect we'll find far more common ground than the loudest voices suggest."

As a transition measure, transfers have been prevented within the first 12 months of commencing a principal course between now and 1 July 2027, when the new transfer visa comes into effect.

Hill also said there will be a "sharpening focus of the skilled migration program" via two new ministerial directions that came into effect last week.

"Priority is now being given to healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing, helping direct skills to the parts of the economy where they are needed most," he said.

The Opposition is expected to announce its immigration policy next week, while One Nation plans to limit net overseas migration to 130,000 per year after three years of "negative migration".

title: Which super funds earned a retirement tick of approval?
text:
in brief An industry assessment handed eight ticks of approval to 45 assessed super funds.

Those eight were found to offer their members the best support through their retirement.

Only eight of 45 assessed superannuation funds have received an industry tick of approval for the level of support they provide members throughout retirement.

The 2026 Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to retirement funds that met at least 14 of an expanded 20 support criteria, up from 18 last year.

The analysis is backed by Chant West, one of Australia's most prominent commercial superannuation research and ratings agencies.

The tick measures how well a fund's investments perform, how competitive its fees are, how innovative its product offerings are, and how comprehensive its member services and advice are.

"Australians have spent decades building their super," said Epic Retirement Institute founder Bec Wilson.

"As they reach retirement, they deserve to understand what their fund can actually do to support them through the years ahead."

The push for better fund support comes as many Australians approach retirement facing significant savings shortfalls.

According to the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, a single homeowner requires $630,000 and a couple $730,000 in super for a "comfortable" retirement.

However, Australian Taxation Office data reveal that the median super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is just over $200,000 — meaning retirees rely heavily on fund advice, tax strategies, and government pension integration to stretch their savings.

Wilson noted that the tick is not a product ranking or a directive to switch membership.

"The Tick is not a rating, ranking or recommendation of a super fund or financial product. There's no first place, second place or 'best fund'," she said.

Instead, it serves as a tool to help Australians "become a more informed super fund member and customer".

Which super funds received the Epic Retirement Tick?

Of 45 assessed regulated, defined-contribution funds, only eight met the benchmark for the 2026/2027 financial year.

Those were:

AMP Super

ART-Super Savings

Aware Super

Brighter Super

Colonial First State - FirstChoice

Hostplus

UniSuper

Vision Super

These funds performed well in several distinct categories, like tailored pension investment options, digital security, and advice access.

AMP, ART, Aware, Hostplus, and Vision Super were highlighted for allowing pension members to request ad-hoc payments and receive funds on the same day or via immediate OSKO transfers.

Funds like ART, AMP, and UniSuper also stood out for offering dedicated lifetime income options like annuities to provide members with guaranteed retirement income.

However, industry analysts note that the overall pass rate remains remarkably low.

Writing in Investment Magazine, Chant West general manager Ian Fryer highlighted that, to earn the badge, funds could no longer rely solely on offering specialised retirement products but also had to demonstrate meaningful member engagement.

For example, funds offering lifetime income options were assessed on whether their members were actually taking up those products.

What has changed this year?

Now in its second year, the Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to three new funds in addition to last year's six — TelstraSuper having merged with Aware. AMP, Colonial, and Vision are all new additions to the benchmark.

The assessment framework has also been updated to target industry difficulties and raise consumer standards. The pass threshold was raised from 12 out of 18 to 14 out of 20, with a new requirement that funds have no outstanding regulatory enforcement actions.

The expanded 2026 criteria introduced tougher hurdles around digital service delivery, complaints management, and cybersecurity protections.

Investment performance criteria were refined to focus on a seven-year evaluation window, rather than 10 years, to allow a stronger emphasis on non-investment support features.

"Some have really stepped up to the plate," Wilson said. "Others are still working towards the standard, and there remains a meaningful gap between what some funds currently provide and what the criteria ask of them."

The Epic Retirement Tick is a proprietary badge issued by a private research firm, not a binding compliance benchmark.

It is separate to statutory government assessment through the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.

title: Card surcharges are banned. Now Aussies are fuming over another charge
text:
In brief Consumers have raised concerns about whether new fees will effectively take the place of card surcharges.

Following an RBA review, businesses can no longer charge customers a surcharge for paying by card.

It took just hours for fresh frustrations to emerge after Australia's card surcharge ban came into effect on Thursday.

Consumers on social media questioned new charges appearing at checkouts online, including some described as "platform" or service fees.

Some said they had encountered the charges in transactions made after new rules came into force preventing businesses from imposing surcharges on credit and debit card payments, prompting questions about whether other fees were effectively taking their place.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) told SBS News it was "aware of concerns about businesses introducing fees described as platform, booking or service fees" since the card surcharge ban took effect.

But the regulator said such fees are not necessarily prohibited.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Whether a charge is a genuine fee for a particular service or amounts to a "card payment surcharge by another name" depends on what it covers and how it operates, an ACCC spokesperson said.

The new rules do not prevent businesses from charging genuine fees for services such as ordering or booking platforms.

However, under Australian Consumer Law, businesses cannot mislead customers about their prices, including the nature or reason for an additional fee or whether it is optional.

Businesses must also display the total minimum price of a product as a single figure, including mandatory fees that can be calculated in advance.

The card surcharge ban followed a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.

In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, consumers should expect to pay $100 at the checkout with either cash or a card.

'Teething issues'

Australian Payments Network chief strategy officer Rajat Jain said a "change of this scale is not immune to some teething issues".

Card networks like Visa and Mastercard, as well as payment service providers, are responsible for administering and enforcing the no-surcharge rules.

Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but they're no longer permitted to add them as an extra fee.

Businesses may choose to reflect those costs in their overall pricing.

"Shoppers shouldn't assume today’s surcharge ban means they'll now start paying less," said Sally Tindall, data insights director of financial comparison site Canstar.

"Businesses still have to pay to accept card payments, so some may choose to build those costs into their prices instead."

For some business owners, the changes have prompted difficult decisions.

David Bitton, owner of the Bitton Rose Bay cafe in Sydney, said more than 90 per cent of his sales are made via card.

With surcharges no longer an option, he estimated the change could cost his business as much as $40,000.

"So I've got to be clever and strategise how I'm gonna pass on that cost, without upsetting people basically," he told SBS News.

Rather than raising menu prices, Bitton said he's increasing his weekend surcharge fee from 10 to 12 per cent.

The RBA says the changes only apply to surcharges specifically added for customers paying by card; booking fees, service fees and hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays are permitted.

Concerned about a fee you've been charged?

Consumers who believe they are still being charged a fee specifically because they paid by card should first seek clarification from the business and ask for the surcharge to be refunded, the ACCC said.

Concerns about ongoing card surcharges can also be raised with the relevant card network or payment service provider.

Jain from the Australian Payments Network said businesses that continue to impose prohibited card surcharges may be directed by their bank or payment provider to remove them and could face penalties.

Meanwhile, concerns about misleading fees or pricing — including a failure to display the total minimum price as a single figure — can be reported to the ACCC or the relevant state or territory consumer protection agency.

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.

The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.

The change applies to both online and in-store transactions.

title: The cockpit question at the heart of the flydubai incident
text:
in brief Passengers were able to access the cockpit of the Flydubai flight as it tumbled from the sky.

Aviation industry experts say the incident raises further questions around airline safety.

This article contains references to suicide.

As authorities attempt to make sense of the flydubai flight that briefly dropped from the sky on Wednesday, a key question will be how passengers were able to enter the cockpit and deal with the threat within it.

The incident, which occurred on a passenger plane travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv in Israel, has raised questions over industry safety.

Since the September 11 attacks, global airline policies have been completely transformed and keeping passengers out of the cockpit was a key focus.

Now, attention will no doubt be turned to the procedures in place to mitigate risks arising from within the flight deck itself — screening and procedures around pilot health and safety will come under scrutiny.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Some of the 174 passengers and crew on board the flydubai flight were able to regain control after the pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, was allegedly stabbed by his co-pilot, who sent the plane into a sharp descent.

As it dropped more than 5km in a matter of minutes, passengers breached the cockpit, took control of the plane, and restrained the co-pilot who had the controls.

The Israeli government has described the incident as a "hijacking" after the emergency call was made from the cockpit by the injured pilot, but flydubai has cautioned against jumping to conclusions. The airline temporarily suspended travel to and from Israel pending a multinational investigation into the incident.

How did passengers manage to breach the cockpit?

Aviation security expert Tony Stanton said access to a passenger plane cockpit should not be possible.

"Whilst the door is not impenetrable, it is highly unlikely that you're able to get through that door," Stanton said.

"Since September 11, there were significant changes to cockpit door security ... it was actually a standard introduced by the United States."

Passengers on board the aircraft said the door to the cockpit — a term which originates in 16th century cock fighting and has been adapted from naval terminology — was open when they approached it.

The Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent altercation in the cockpit. Source: Getty / Erik Marmor

"The door apparently wasn't locked and we managed to open it somehow," passenger Yaniv Hayoun told reporters.

Hayoun later told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that as others tied up the attacker, "I jumped back, grabbed the controls, and started pulling back the handles", before other crew members took over.

Stanton said pilots in the cockpit typically need to press a button inside to open the door. He suspects Machchhar was able to do this while injured.

Former A380 Airbus captain James Nixon said the pilot had "amazing" presence of mind in thinking to open the door after having been stabbed.

"Even if the cabin crew wanted to get in to help, they would firstly go through a procedure where the pilots have to let them in," he told ABC News on Thursday.

"There's another procedure that takes about 35 or 40 seconds to get in if there's no response.

"So, it would have taken a long time, and by that stage it would have all been over."

Incident shines a light on pilot mental health

While the motivation of the co-pilot in the flydubai incident is unclear, Stanton notes that mental health incidents with pilots are becoming more common.

In 2022 a China Eastern flight carrying 132 people was intentionally plunged into the ground in China by someone in the cockpit, black box data later found, killing everyone on board.

In 2015, a Germanwings flight from Barcelona to Düsseldorf was intentionally directed into the French Alps by its 27-year-old pilot, who had previously been treated for severe suicidal tendencies. All 150 people on board were killed.

READ MORE The 15 minutes that plunged a flydubai flight into chaos: What we know

"They're still very, very rare, but they're starting to happen more often," Stanton said.

Screening for pilot mental health in Australia is governed by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), which relies on a combination of mandatory periodic health assessments and regular examinations conducted by specialist medical teams.

While the process is rigorous and the industry has extensive safety procedures in place to screen for troubled staff, Stanton argued that "a questionnaire on a screen every year" is not sufficient.

"Pilots are afraid of reporting things because if CASA takes away their medical, you don't have a job," he said. "Pilots are incredibly reluctant, sadly, to disclose some things when they go and do this yearly check."

However, he said there is no way to make flying completely risk-free and that aircraft incidents will continue as passenger numbers across the globe are only projected to increase.

"Even if we kept the accident rate the same today, if it's the same in 20 years, we will have more catastrophes simply because we're increasing the amount we fly."

title: Want permanent residency in Japan? Here's how the rules are getting tougher
text:
In brief Foreigners seeking Japanese permanent residency will face tougher rules including higher fees.

The reforms are part of a tightening of immigration controls by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Japan has toughened requirements for foreigners seeking permanent residency as part of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to tighten immigration controls.

Under new rules that will come into effect in stages, foreign residents wishing to stay in Japan permanently will have to prove their annual income is above average and they can carry casual conversations in Japanese.

Application fees will also rise 20-fold from Thursday (from 10,000 yen ($91) to 200,000 yen ($1,800).

At one immigration office in central Tokyo visited by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency this week, hundreds of people queued, hoping to wrap up procedures before the price spike.

"I understand that over-accepting foreigners ... might dilute Japan's unique culture. But at the same time, given its low birth rate and aging population, Japan has to accept foreigners," said US-born university student Yujie Chono, who was among those waiting.

The 22-year-old told AFP, in fluent Japanese, that he had been waiting for five hours to file his paperwork.

Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills.

Even though Japan has a rapidly ageing population and is suffering labour shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.

"As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness," Takaichi said in an extended post on X on Sunday, adding that she was pushing for "orderly coexistence" with foreign nationals.

Programs to attract international workers have fuelled public worry.

Anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan go to foreigners and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.

Experts and many business leaders warn, however, that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.

Japan needs to open its doors to more foreigners, the Nikkei business daily said in a recent editorial.

"Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment," it said.

Anti-immigration sentiment

Foreigners were a major issue in last year's upper house election, which saw the sharp rise of the "Japanese-first" Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a "silent invasion".

The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs will be forced to leave Japan if they don't meet the new conditions.

Some foreign residents seek permanent residency to secure long-term stability, employment freedom and to earn trust within Japanese society. Those without permanent residency often have difficulty obtaining mortgages, for example.

Thursday's changes may prevent some people from applying for permanent residency but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.

Candidates must also show "understanding" of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

Having lived in Japan for a decade, permanent residency applicant Chono said he saw both sides of the debate but that the country needed young people "to support its future".

"In recent years, I believe there had been a strong push to promote cultural diversity. The momentum has stalled, perhaps, and maybe it may never fully return."

title: The Roosters lost the 2025 grand final without her. This time, Tarryn Aiken won’t let title slip
text:
Roosters halfback Tarryn Aiken returns to the NRLW grand final after missing the 2025 decider with an ACL injury.

Tarryn Aiken doesn’t lose her cool often. So when she does, you listen. “If she’s spraying you, you know we’re all doing something wrong,” says teammate Olivia Kernick. There hasn’t been much wrong with the Roosters this season, which means Aiken’s sprays have been few and far between. But they’ve certainly been memorable. “It happened in the Raiders game,” Kernick begins. Not the Raiders game just gone, where the Roosters won 20-10 in last weekend’s preliminary final to progress to their third grand final in three years. Kernick is referring to the round-three clash the Roosters described as a “loss in our eyes”, even though they won, and have remained undefeated all season. Tarryn Aiken speaks at a grand final fan day on Friday. Getty Images “It was pretty funny,” concedes Kernick. “It was pretty early on. We don’t really hear from her, she’s very calm, cool and collected on field.”

Advertisement

It’s difficult to find fault with an unbeaten season, but if you want to nitpick then that’s the match to look at. The Roosters have trailed for a combined 70 minutes and two seconds all season, but nearly half of that was during the round-three match in Canberra. It prompted the Tricolours to wipe the whiteboard clean and start their season all over again. “I think we probably learnt a lot about ourselves in that game, and what works for us as a team,” Aiken says. “We had gone away and experimented with a few things before that game. But after that game, we went back to the drawing board and worked. Spoke about what strengths are good for our team and as individual players and went back to our strengths as a team.” And what are those strengths? “Can’t tell you that,” Aiken says with a smirk.

Advertisement

Ask others, however, and they’ll tell you the Roosters are strongest when Aiken is calling the shots. “She’s the best half in the game,” says captain Isabelle Kelly. “She gets a lot of recognition, but the way that she can read the game, attacking-wise, and create situations for the people outside of her, is really incredible.” Aiken was a notable absence in last year’s grand final, having suffered an ACL injury in the last round of the regular season which ruled her out of the finals. The Roosters lost the decider to Brisbane in the final five minutes of the match. Tarryn Aiken is assisted from the field after injuring her ACL in round 11 of the 2025 season. Getty Images Jocelyn Kelleher and Corban Baxter had been admirable when filling in at No.7. But Aiken had been the team’s X-factor, and her loss cost them dearly. “To lose your halfback two weeks out from a grand final, it’s obviously insanely hard considering we had her all year,” Kelleher says. “I was lucky enough to be trusted with that spot. However, we are a lot stronger when she’s back. She gets through holes that don’t even exist, and she’s a genius out on that field.”

Advertisement

That ability to step up when the game is on the line was on full display last weekend, when Aiken slipped through a crack in the Raiders defence to score the clinching try. Loading For Aiken, who had helped orchestrate the Broncos’ premierships in 2019 and 2020 and then for the Roosters in 2024, missing last year’s finals was the hardest moment of her career. “It was a tough week for me, personally, missing out on finals and the grand final,” says Aiken. “Career-wise, that was definitely the hardest part, missing the finals last year and then obviously the lengthy rehab.” She’s a nervous spectator, which made it difficult to sit on the sideline and watch, powerless, as the premiership slipped away. One thing stood out when the Knights interviewed Justin Holbrook: his vision for the club was clear. Three parties registered to bid for the keys to M601/68 McEvoy Street, with all active. Bidding opening at $850,000 followed by increments of $10,000 and $5000 before the hammer fell and the property sold. It had a guide of $900,000 and an adjusted reserve of $975,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.

The underbidders live locally and were hoping to upsize from a one-bedroom apartment. They had made a pre-auction offer of $900,000 but the vendors, who have already bought elsewhere, chose to proceed to auction. The open-plan kitchen and dining space includes a built-in laundry. While it comes with a car space, you don’t need to leave the building to do the grocery shopping. Domain The new owner was attracted to the size of the 95-square-metre apartment, which includes a north-facing balcony, as well as the proximity of the IGA supermarket, which is in the building. Sales agent for Ray White Erskineville, Moira Verheijen said this week’s interest rate rise had created further “cautiousness” in the market. “Interest rates have definitely had an impact,” she said.

Some buyers think they can wait because it feels like [the market] is continuing to go down but if they wait, those quality homes may not be there.” The property was one of 216 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Baulkham Hills, a young family won the keys to a three-bedroom home, paying $140,000 above the reserve.

Bidding for 23 Merinda Avenue opened at $1.3 million, followed by two bids of $50,000, and then increments of $10,000 and $5000 until the property sold for $1.59 million. Seven parties registered to bid for the property, which had a guide of $1.4 million and a reserve of $1.45 million, with four active. The successful bidders were a local young family who plan to rent out the property before renovating. The vendor is going into aged care. Sales agent for McGrath Castle Hill, Jamie Benjamin, said buyers were attracted by the location, close to transport and schools, rather than the house itself. “Most [buyers] ruled it out because the property was not, essentially, liveable,” he said. “But it’s a classic family location.”

title: Stephen King didn’t want another Carrie remake. This is what convinced him
text:
A new Carrie is upon us, but she’s not exactly what you’d expect.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first glance, Summer H. Howell and Stephen King’s Carrie White have nothing in common. One is a soft-spoken 22-year-old Canadian actor. The other is a traumatised telekinetic teen who destroys her hometown in a vengeful rage. Related Article ★★★★

Review This is the most brutal retelling of Carrie yet They do, however, share one key experience: they both spent their first prom covered in blood. Howell missed her high school dance – or “grad” as they call it in Canada – because she’d been working. Little did she know she’d stumble upon a second chance while filming the lead role in Carrie, Mike Flanagan’s TV adaptation of King’s seminal horror novel. “I had a wonderful prom,” Howell says with fond reminiscence and a hint of trauma. “It feels like one big fever dream ... I had about 11 days covered in blood, head to toe. I did a lot of relying on other people and sitting, trying not to mess up my continuity … It was really cool to get to experience it in a way.” Loading The “Black Prom” is one of the most famous sequences in horror history. It began, of course, with King’s 1974 debut novel, which introduced the image of Carrie doused in pigs’ blood following a cruel prank. It’s the pivotal moment in a story about an outcast teen who faces relentless bullying by schoolmates and a fanatically religious mother before unleashing her telekinetic powers in a fit of destruction.

Advertisement

Equal parts horrifying and tragic, the scene has been recreated many times including in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film with Sissy Spacek and the 2013 movie starring Chloë Grace Moretz and Julianne Moore. It’s even had several incarnations in a stage musical. Sissy Spacek during the iconic “Black Prom” scene in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Alamy Stock Photo Chloë Grace Moretz wreaks havoc in the 2013 film version of Carrie. In other words, the story has been told – exhaustively. So, when Amazon Prime Video pitched Flanagan the idea of adapting Carrie for the small screen, the showrunner’s first instinct was to turn it down. Not only was it not on his King adaptation wishlist, he also generally avoids remakes and sequels, opting instead for fresh source material like Gerald’s Game and The Haunting of Hill House. Stephen King was also sceptical. The horror legend believed there was no need for more Carrie. “He said, I think it’s been done’,” Flanagan recalls. “And I said ‘I think I agree’.” The filmmaker wouldn’t proceed without King’s stamp of approval. But an idea kept niggling at him. “Teenagers today deal with cruelty and anxiety to a degree [Stephen King] never could have contemplated 50 years ago.” Carrie showrunner Mike Flanagan “I couldn’t stop thinking about it,” Flanagan says. “It’s been half a century since Stephen King created that character and that story in that world, but so much of what he was talking about is more relevant today than it was when he wrote it.”

Advertisement

“Teenagers today deal with cruelty and anxiety to a degree Steve never could have contemplated 50 years ago – that I couldn’t contemplate when I was growing up. I never went to school afraid I could be killed there.” When Flanagan had his “Carrie moments”, he notes that they also remained largely private. His “most vulnerable, humiliating and defining moments” weren’t preserved digitally forever, in full view on the internet. Teenagers today can’t relate. So what would happen if Carrie were dropped in the age of TikTok and rampant school shootings? Related Article Streaming The most exciting book adaptations coming to TV this year Flanagan, who’s renowned for his emotional, character-driven horrors like The Fall of the House of Usher and Oculus, came up with what he calls the “anti-Carrie”. While De Palma’s lead character was traumatised from the moment the cameras started rolling, Flanagan’s is more of an “unspoiled heart”. “We created a character who came into the world with trust, eagerness and openness – with a fearlessness socially and a genuine belief in the goodness of the environment around her. She then reacts to the realities we’ve all normalised in society for teenagers,” he says. This, it turns out, was enough to convince Stephen King. But with that hurdle overcome, the next presented itself: finding the new Carrie White.

Advertisement

Flanagan, along with King as an executive producer, searched for someone who embodied an earnest curiosity without being naive, and a vulnerability paired with hidden strength. More than 1400 people auditioned for the role, making it the biggest casting effort of Flanagan’s career to date. Mike Flanagan had no idea how they were going to find his perfect Carrie White. Then Summer H. Howell appeared. Robert Falconer/Prime They searched tirelessly until, finally, Howell emerged. She had never read or seen previous versions of Carrie, which ironically worked in her favour. After sharing countless self-tapes, Howell was offered the role – on April Fools’ Day. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘That’s got to count for something’: Julia Morris and Julia Zemiro on four decades in the spotlight “I was just like, ‘What’s happening? What a funny joke that would be’,” she says. “I always assume with big projects that you’re up against a lot of people. But I just put it out of mind and did my own thing.” Her reaction was a combination of shock, honour and a fair deal of intimidation. Carrie is legendary, after all. “But because I hadn’t been influenced by any other version of her, I found it to be really fun,” she says. “I just tried to have a good time with it and enjoy the ride.” Carrie isn’t the only character to undergo a refresh. Adopting more of a YA slant, the series offers a glimpse into the home-life of other key characters, including Carrie’s mother Margaret White, famously played by Piper Laurie in the 1976 film. Here, she’s played by Samantha Sloyan and is no longer a monster. Rather, she’s a product of her own abuse.

Advertisement

Summer H. Howell (left) and Samantha Sloyan (right) in the new Carrie series. Liane Hentscher/ Prime “Where Sam [Sloyan] takes it is so heartbreaking, so beautiful and so human,” Flanagan says. “The late season scenes between her and Summer are some of my favourite I’ve ever witnessed on a set of mine in my life. I’m very interested in the cyclical nature of abuse and trauma, and the self-sustaining nature of that.” Carrie’s main bully, Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton), is given similar treatment. She isn’t just a “mean girl monster”; she’s reacting to her own deep well of pain, largely caused by her parents’ divorce (her mother is played by Heather Graham) and money issues. This is the source of her poor choices, such as filming Carrie sobbing in the school showers after getting her first period. Instead of helping her, Hargensen chants “plug it up” and shares the footage on an anonymous account online, turning Carrie into the school’s laughingstock. “There really are no monsters in frame, at least not in the beginning,” Flanagan says. “And if we ever meet a monster, we get to see how they’re made.” Chris Hargensen, played by Alison Thornton (right) doesn’t simply play a “mean girl monster” in Mike Flanagan’s version of Carrie. Robert Falconer/Prime As horrific as scenes like this sound, it’s actually not that far off the experience of many contemporary US teens. Flanagan opened his writers’ room to actual high schoolers to hear their lived experience of bullying, gun violence and social media. Demonstrating the human side of horror is signature Flanagan. But it’s also something he picked up from King, who he describes as a “humanist and optimist”.

PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘This puts us in hospitals’: Victorian riders demand action on potholes Brielle Kohlbeck October 3, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For longtime motorcyclist Michael White, his bike isn’t just transportation, it’s his way of life. White recently finished up a 4000-kilometre ride through Victoria, South Australia and New South Wales and says he saw more potholes in the first 20 minutes coming back into Victoria than he did in all the other states combined. Motorcyclists Ilona Szabo and Irene Gianelli are worried about potholes. Jason South He and Paul Povh began their biker podcast, Hogs, Cogs and Two Aussie Flogs, in 2020. They were only six months in when they began speaking out about the issue of Victorian roads. According to the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office, almost half of Victoria’s roads are in poor or very poor condition – and White says motorcyclists are the ones paying for it.

Advertisement

“We know riding motorcycles is dangerous, more dangerous than driving a car,” White says. “But give us a fighting chance, for God’s sake. That’s what we’re asking for, a fighting chance to get home to our families.” Related Article Roads Almost half of Victoria’s roads in poor condition, as decline outpaces repairs “If a car hits a big pothole, it’s annoying at most,” White says. “More often than not it might mean a bent rim or a flat tyre. This puts us in hospitals.” Following the death of motorcyclist Peter “Tiki” Mason after he hit a pothole near Trawalla on September 13, the issue of the state’s broken roads has taken on a new urgency. White briefly met Mason at the Redback Rally motorcycle gathering in February. He describes the 71-year-old rider as a gentleman, describing how he helped female motorcycle riders and even used to escort bullied kids to school.

Advertisement

Related Series

Victorian election Victoria’s pothole crisis “I only spoke to him for about 20 minutes, and he left an impression on me,” White said. “I’m just glad I was lucky enough to meet him.” Rob Salvatore, the chair of the Victorian Motorcycle Council, the premier advocacy body working on behalf of motorcyclists, believes the issue comes down to a matter of resources, funding and the standards applied to the road repairs. “The government has responded by trying to increase resources but clearly, as pointed out by the Victorian Auditor-General’s report, it is lagging behind,” Salvatore said. Roads are one of the biggest issues on the table for the November 28 election. Premier Ben Carroll plans to have prisoners put on road maintenance in response to the problem, while the Coalition is pledging to fix 1 million potholes with a $5 billion funding increase.

Advertisement

“With this current government there’s a lot of mistrust,” said Ilona Szabo, a relatively new motorcyclist based in Melbourne’s western suburbs. “It’s been a long time since anything has been properly done for the roads.” Szabo started riding only four years ago but has quickly become engaged in the community. About two years in, she created a women-only riding group for her and surrounding suburbs. She met Irene Giannelli through her group, and both are disappointed with the way road issues aren’t being addressed. Paul Povh (left) and Michael White, at the riders’ protest outside Parliament House after Peter “Tiki” Mason died, are organising a “broken roads rally” for October 4. Ruby Alexander “Somebody’s got to do something,” Giannelli said. “With most politicians as well, they say all these things, and they never follow through.”

Advertisement

According to a spokesman for the Office of the Premier, the government has invested more than $40 million as part of its Motorcycle Safety Infrastructure Program, which funds motorcycle safety improvements at high-risk sites across the state. Labor is promising further action if it wins the November election. Related Article Roads The small holes making big news: An unscientific reckoning on Victoria’s roads “A re-elected Labor government will also deliver a comprehensive plan to improve the quality of our roads and how we fix them,” said Roads Minister Paul Hamer. Motorcyclists don’t plan to wait for the election. White and Povh are organising a “broken roads rally” on October 4, calling on motorcyclists to head to Parliament to demand action on the roads and honour “fallen riders”. Szabo, Giannelli and plenty of other motorcyclists plan to attend.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
